I will reverse it and set it in the east,” which is of your own attribute, even though from it there is normally no physical birth in this world.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Batra 16a: ‘Reish Lakish says: Satan, the evil inclination, and the Angel of Death are one, that is, they are three aspects of the same essence. He is the Satan who seduces people and then accuses them, as it is written: “So the Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord, and smote Job with vile sores” (Job 2:7). He is also the evil inclination, as it is written there: “The impulse of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continuously” (Genesis 6:5); and it is written here: “Only upon himself do not put forth your hand” (Job 1:12). The verbal analogy between the various uses of the word “only” teaches that the evil inclination is to be identified with the Satan. He is also the Angel of Death,…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:24, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 16a) to illuminate his teaching here (“it is as our Sages of blessed memory said Bava Batra 16a: he is the Satan, he is the evil inclination, he is the Angel of Death; and "evil pursues the sinners" Proverbs 13:21. Therefore Noah sent the raven into the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this prosecutorial entity is itself the force of the evil inclination, as our Sages taught (Bava Batra 16a): "He is Satan, he is the evil inclination: he descends [and seduces, ascends and accuses, receives permission and takes the soul]". The meaning: when it resides Above, the concept of an earthly evil urge does not apply, its power functioning there as accusation—which is contrary to Hashem's true will, for He desires beneficence and despises anyone who slanders His children, as the Sages noted.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 41:4
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And these three nations were enumerated first, corresponding to Edom, Ammon, and Moab (Bava Batra 56a), and that is: if they can conquer these three, we understand from this that they have already refined themselves in the seven attributes within their strength. And from observing that they could not dispossess the seven nations completely, it indicates that they had not yet perfected themselves completely in the seven attributes; therefore Hashem did not deliver unto them these three.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 13:21: ‘Misfortune pursues sinners,But the righteous are well rewarded.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:24, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 13:21) to illuminate his teaching here (“and "evil pursues the sinners" Proverbs 13:21. Therefore Noah sent the raven into the world before the dove, just as Esau preceded Jacob, for the shell always precedes the fruit.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is "evil pursues sinners" (Proverbs 13:21), and "I have created the waster to destroy" (Isaiah 54:16), and as written in Bereishit Rabbah 6: fire issues from the bodies of the wicked and consumes them, and among plants: lethal poison, may the Merciful One spare us, and the like. And in proportion to the closeness or distance of the extension of his light and vitality within them, such is their relationship to him: some remain his permanent possessions; some were in his possession for a time and he sold them.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “The wicked are overthrown, and are not”—this is the Generation of the Flood; “but the house of the righteous shall stand”—this is Noah. My revered father, of blessed memory (Mei HaShiloach, Vol. 2, Proverbs 10, s.v. Ka'avor), explained this: when the Blessed Name conducts His world in a garment termed “whirlwind” (sufah)—meaning through the concentrated intensity of a single attribute— the righteous aligned with that attribute surge in tremendous power that the generation finds hard to bear.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Exodus 35:3: ‘You shall kindle no fire throughout your settlements on the sabbath day.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Exodus 35:3) to illuminate his teaching here (“Exodus 35:3 "You shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations" Parashat Vayakhel: "Though I sit in darkness, Hashem is a light unto me" Micah 7:8. Fire is awe, shining in the dark;”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For the Name Elohim has a plural grammatical form, signifying that He encompasses all diverse cosmic powers, as written in Tur, Orach Chayim (sec. 5); that is, through the contraction (tzimtzum) concealing His absolute Unity, the cosmos was created displaying differentiated natural forces; whereas the Tetragrammaton indicates He was, He is, and He will be, denoting that even in the present He remains solitary and One just as prior to Creation.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” This is what Scripture states (Psalms 84:12): “For a sun and shield is the Lord God; grace and glory does the Lord bestow; He withholds no good from those who walk uprightly.” It is taught in the Holy Zohar (Pekudei 224b): “Sun”—this is the mystery of the Holy Name Havayah, wherein all spiritual rungs abide in serene rest; “and shield”—this is the mystery of the Holy Name termed Elohim, corresponding to the secret of the verse (Genesis 15:1): “I am a shield to you”.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Micah 7:8: ‘Do not rejoice over me,O my enemy! Though I have fallen, I rise again;Though I sit in darkness, GOD is my light.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Micah 7:8) to illuminate his teaching here (“"Though I sit in darkness, Hashem is a light unto me" Micah 7:8. Fire is awe, shining in the dark; but what does a candle achieve in bright daylight Chullin 60b for one to whom Havayah is his light,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And precisely from there "will the Lord your God gather you, and from there will He fetch you" (Devarim 30:4); for the supernal Light is a light that shines even within the darkness, clarifying that "all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings" (Shemos 10:23) even in the days of darkness; for "though I sit in darkness, Hashem shall be a light unto me" (Michah 7:8), and "yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Tehillim 23:4).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And from it inner fortitude is born in man to attain divine service, granting enduring existence to all creations. Therefore until this Name was invoked the sprouts stood halted at the soil's surface (Chullin 60b). A parable: man possesses senses of sight, hearing, and the like, which are unified within the soul; yet when expressed through individual physical organs, they disperse into specific faculties, each organ exhibiting only a fraction of power; whereas enfolded together in the soul, man holds immense unified vigor.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Chullin 60b: ‘She said before Him: Master of the Universe, since I said a correct observation before You, must I diminish myself? God said to her: As compensation, go and rule both during the day along with the sun and during the night. She said to Him: What is the greatness of shining alongside the sun? What use is a candle in the middle of the day? God said to her: Go; let the Jewish people count the days and years with you, and this will be your greatness. She said to Him: But the Jewish people will count with the sun as well, as it is impossible that they will not count seasons with it, as it is written: “And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years” (Genesis 1:14). God said…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Chullin 60b) to illuminate his teaching here (“but what does a candle achieve in bright daylight Chullin 60b for one to whom Havayah is his light, as in "For a sun and a shield is Hashem" and fire is the cooking rectification of all food;”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Then that lesser light is subsumed, along the lines of: "What does a small lamp profit at high noon?" (Chullin 60b). However, the essence of Purim, does not represent liberation from merely a specific temporal vice, but deliverance from the universal root of evil, 'Amalek, the first of the nations', who denies the transcendent Root.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And the primary awakening for the creation of man emerged from the collective plea of all creations, who recognized that they lacked a leader and mediating bridge between Hashem and themselves. And so we find in the Gemara (Chullin 60b): “This teaches that the vegetation stood at the threshold of the ground”; meaning that all creations clamored, declaring that while latent power existed within them, to bring forth manifest salvation was impossible without man.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Psalms 84:12: ‘For the ETERNAL God is sun and shield; GOD bestows grace and glory,and does not withhold bounty from those who live without blame.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Psalms 84:12) to illuminate his teaching here (“as in "For a sun and a shield is Hashem" and fire is the cooking rectification of all food; except that most fruits are eaten raw; and concerning wine there is a dispute whether raw is superior to cooked,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this current exile preparing for the World to Come is the drawing of blood and the beginning of healing, and when the healing of the world's mortal stroke is completed, we will merit the World to Come—the mystery of the eighth day— which is the perfection of the covenant in the flesh, the body being consecrated to enter the Supernal Land and merit eternal life.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And sun and shield”—this signifies the mystery of the Complete Name [Havayah Elohim]; “grace and glory does the Lord bestow”—so that all becomes unified in a single mystery. “Sun” is the Name Havayah, designated as the sun; and from the aspect of this Name alone, no created entity could possibly emerge into independent existence in the world, for all would remain nullified within His immense supernal light.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 39b: ‘In connection to the various halakhot with regard to breaking bread, especially on Festivals, the Gemara cites another halakha. Rabbi Abba said: And on Shabbat one is obligated to break bread for the meal over two loaves. What is the reason? Because in the Torah portion that discusses gathering manna on Friday for Shabbat, the phrase: “Twice as much bread” (Exodus 16:22) is written. To commemorate this, Shabbat meals are based on two loaves of bread.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 39b) to illuminate his teaching here (“see Tosafot, chapter Keitzad Mevarechin, Berakhot 39b, for: "Is not My word like fire", the light of Torah shines and requires no earthly fire; and salted food corresponds to suffering,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Now, King Solomon, peace be upon him—whose name signifies wholeness (Shelomoh / shalom) and whose teaching was consummate (see Berakhot 39b) — yearned to attain the ultimate summit of spiritual perfection, as is known, and as written in the Zohar, that in his reign the moon stood in its full, luminous perfection (kayma sihara b'shleimuta).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Yet in truth, beyond human perception, even within vegetation an enduring spiritual spark remains, as it is written: “And to every beast of the earth” with a connective Vav, and this is because they yearned for the creation of man; as taught in the Gemara (Chullin 60b): “This teaches that the vegetation stood at the threshold of the soil until Adam came and pleaded for mercy upon them.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Jeremiah 23:29: ‘Behold, My word is like fire—declares GOD—and like a hammer that shatters rock!’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Jeremiah 23:29) to illuminate his teaching here (“for: "Is not My word like fire", the light of Torah shines and requires no earthly fire; and salted food corresponds to suffering, as written in the first chapter of Berakhot 5a: it is like cooked,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Fire licking his bench: the fire of his Torah, for "Is not My word like as a fire?" (Yirmiyah 23:29); and "Torah scholars, their entire body is fire, wherefore the fire of Gehinnom has no power over them" (Chagigah 27a). And this is the ultimate pinnacle of Israel's holiness: that even the Temple Mount, devoid today of physical sacrificial service, remains holy unto our Master with immutable sanctity; and even the most degraded in Israel, even one descending into the valley of the shadow of death: "I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Tehillim 23:4).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For behold, it is written (Jeremiah 23:24): “Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? says the Lord”; what then was the nature of Noah's concealment within the Ark? However, they resolved this in the Holy Zohar (Noach 64b): “And if you ask, how were Noah and those with him delivered? He was hidden from the eye, and therefore when He destroyed the world, he was not remembered in the decree of judgment, being hidden from sight.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 5a: ‘Previously, the Gemara discussed suffering that results from one’s transgressions. The Gemara shifts the focus and discusses suffering that does not result from one’s transgressions and the suffering of the righteous. Rava, and some say Rav Ḥisda, said: If a person sees that suffering has befallen him, he should examine his actions. Generally, suffering comes about as punishment for one’s transgressions, as it is stated: “We will search and examine our ways, and return to God” (Lamentations 3:40). If he examined his ways and found no transgression for which that suffering is appropriate, he may attribute his suffering to dereliction in the study of Torah. God punishes an individual for…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 5a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in the first chapter of Berakhot 5a: it is like cooked, for suffering brings to awe; and this is the reality of the Sabbath day. And nevertheless, one must toil in the cooking of food on the eve of Shabbat;”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: But he did not realize that he had already returned the entire blemish to its unholy place; wherefore Hashem departed from upon him, for the holiness within his heart had become enfeebled; and his heart could no longer serve as a sanctuary for His Shechinah like the Holy of Holies! The theme: The phrase "as at other times" pointing to the three initial trials, the yetzer hara solidifying into a master after three encounters, and Samson as the dawn of Mashiach. Samson's words "as at other times" refer specifically to the three previous occasions when he trifled with Delilah.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Therefore prior to this Adam was not commanded regarding the Tree of Knowledge, for he was like an unborn child that produces no waste and cannot sin. Only after Adam prayed for rain on behalf of all creations, bringing creation from potential into actualized deed, as in Chullin (60b): “This teaches that the vegetation stood at the threshold of the soil” — did the true birth of Adam in this world take place, attaining maturity as an agent of free choice, capable of acting contrary to the divine Will.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Avodah Zarah 3a: ‘The Gemara asks: And how can you say so, that it is possible to perform a mitzva after the end of this world? But doesn’t Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi say: What is the meaning of that which is written: “You shall therefore keep the commandment, and the statutes, and the ordinances, which I command you this day, to do them” (Deuteronomy 7:11)? This verse teaches that today, in this world, is the time to do them, but tomorrow, in the World-to-Come, is not the time to do them. Furthermore, today is the time to do them, but today is not the time to receive one’s reward, which is granted in the World-to-Come.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Avodah Zarah 3a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written at the beginning of the first chapter of Avodah Zarah 3a–4b: "this day to do them"—and tomorrow to receive their reward; for this divine light does not come automatically to man. And likewise the Shabbat...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Unlike the World to Come which is likened to day (Pesachim 2b), wherein no disruption of order will exist, free from shifts caused by fluctuating deeds. The Sages having taught (Avodah Zarah 3a): "'This day to do them' [Deuteronomy 7:11]—and not tomorrow to do them." But in this world of action where free choice rests in human hands, the order shifts through human conduct: falling into adversity, afflictions, and exile through wickedness; and rising to good through cleaving unto the Blessed Name Who rules over worlds and guiding angels, transforming their names and courses.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 56:3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Meaning that vigilance he had already possessed from before, and through vigilance he now arrived at alacrity, as brought in the Talmud (Avodah Zarah 20b): “Vigilance leads to alacrity”; and Hashem illuminated unto Avraham that everything he had enacted until now was in the mystery of 'Shamor' (Keep/Restrain), and now he merited the mystery of 'Zakhor' (Remember/Active alacrity).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Deuteronomy 7:11: ‘Therefore, observe faithfully the Instruction—the laws and the rules—with which I charge you today.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 7:11) to illuminate his teaching here (“"this day to do them"—and tomorrow to receive their reward; for this divine light does not come automatically to man. And likewise the Shabbat lamp must be kindled on the eve of Shabbat, but on Shabbat itself there...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Therefore Scripture used regarding Purim the language of "and rest, etc." (Esther 9:22), terming it rest and serenity akin to Shabbat; for as long as man requires exertion and outward action he has no true serenity, and therefore this world is full of distraction and toil, and when a person passes away, "his soul rested", and the World to Come is a day that is entirely Shabbat and rest, wherein "the righteous sit crowned, etc." (Berakhot 17a), for "today is for performing them, and tomorrow is for receiving their reward" (Avodah Zarah 3a).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Yet from creation’s perspective it is preferable to receive everything through moral screening and boundaries, which corresponds to the ripened fruit. And this parallels what is stated in the Gemara (Berakhot 31a): “The daughters of Israel acted stringently upon themselves, that even if they see a drop of blood as small as a mustard seed, they observe seven clean days.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 35b: ‘Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina, said: I heard that a person who was pressed for time and comes to light Shabbat lights after six blasts may light without concern, as even the moment of the sixth blast is not yet Shabbat. Proof for this is that the Sages provided the sexton of the synagogue a period of time to take his shofar, which he used to sound the blasts on a tall roof in the middle of the city, to his house. Clearly, during that interval it is not yet Shabbat. He said to him: If so, then you have rendered your statement subject to circumstances, and it would not apply uniformly to all. Shabbat would start at a different time in each place based on the distance between the site where the…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 35b) to illuminate his teaching here (“as they said Shabbat 35b: provided that one does not light too early, etc.; analogous to the birth pangs of the Messiah adjacent to the footsteps of the Messiah, for cleaving and love always immediately follow awe....”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: To be simultaneously zealous where zeal is required for Hashem's will, and restrained/passive where one must hold back— this dual balance is impossible through the natural inclination alone; and one who is naturally zealous will rush also to commit evil, and one who is sluggish will be slothful also regarding good deeds. And the spiritual differentiation occurs through the dormant falls intervening in between, and he strengthens and overcomes with all his might when he returns, remembers, and awakens from his sleep.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 12:5 (§2)
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For only where unity and love dwell among creatures does Hashem cause the Shechinah of His glory to dwell. However where violence and robbery are heard: “Now will I rise, says Hashem, now will I be exalted” from dwelling in this world, as written (Psalms 57:12): “Be exalted, O God, above the heavens, etc.” And it is taught on this in the holy Zohar (Noach 48b): Rabbi Abba opened: “'Be exalted above the heavens, etc.'— woe to the wicked who sin, etc., pushing the Shechinah from the earth and causing Her to depart from the world.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yoma 72b: ‘The Gemara asks: But wasn’t it taught in a baraita that the outer ark was eleven handbreadths and a bit? The Gemara explains: This is not difficult: This statement in the baraita is in accordance with the one who said that the thickness of the gold plating was one handbreadth. According to this opinion, the outer ark’s base took up one handbreadth of its height, ten handbreadths were then needed to contain the middle ark within it, and then a bit more was needed so it could also contain the Ark’s cover. That statement of Rav Yehuda is in accordance with the one who said that the thickness of the gold plating was not one handbreadth but was a plate of gold of negligible thickness.…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 72b) to illuminate his teaching here (“And so our Sages of blessed memory stated in Yoma 72b: concerning Torah: if fear of Hashem is his treasure, it serves as the outer keys. And 'sitting/settling' everywhere denotes delay and cessation from active...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Therefore one's fear of sin must precede his wisdom, as stated in Avot, for otherwise it cannot endure, and "if there is no fear, there is no wisdom." And this explains why the Talmud in Shabbat first likened it to outer keys, and then conversely likened fear to the inner courtyard and Torah to the outer gate, which appears contradictory—presenting fear as inner and Torah as the entryway—alongside the mishnaic dictum in Avot: "If there is no wisdom, there is no fear."
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And to this points the prefix Mem in “me'asot (from doing)... mi-metzo (from finding)”—indicating an abrupt cessation in the middle of an act. The rationale being: during weekdays, even as man expands within the garment, a minute memory of the inner essence remains preserved; but were he to finalize the outer garment on the Sabbath day, he would completely forget the divine Root that animates it, clinging to an alienated shell.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 84:3: ‘“If a lash causes death suddenly” (Job 9:23) – Antoninos asked Rabbeinu, he said to him: ‘What is the meaning of what is written: “If a lash causes death suddenly”?’ Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi] said: ‘[If you were to] decree that one should receive one hundred lashes and they would give him one hundred dinars. The total of this is the total of that, but he will not get anything from him, and in that way he makes a mockery of the one receiving the lashes. “He mocks at the undoing of the innocent” (Job 9:23) – Rav Aḥa said: When the righteous live in tranquility and seek to live in tranquility in this world,). the accuser comes and accuses them. He says: Is what is prepared for them in the World…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 84:3) to illuminate his teaching here (“and this is what our Sages said Bereishit Rabbah 84:3: Jacob sought to settle in serenity, for every 'sitting' implies restful tranquility and he meant: Jacob sought to attain the level of the World to Come”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And even though it was foreseen before Him and He beheld all future corruptions, He did not refrain from creating the world; for the sake of Israel who are the primary purpose of Creation, within whom everything is transformed into good, even their sins; following rectification the primordial depth and the ultimate depth being revealed as entirely good, whereby all intermediate stumbling is sweetened!
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Refusing to grasp the Name Shaddai—which signifies constriction and the harmonious integration of attributes—in order to acquire an everlasting edifice. And this is what the Sages stated (Sanhedrin 108a): The final decree against the Generation of the Flood was sealed only when they stretched forth their hands in robbery, as said: “for the earth is filled with violence through them, and, behold, I will destroy them with the earth”; and in Midrash Rabbah (Behar 33:3): A measuring-basket full of iniquities—who prosecutes at the head? Robbery, as said: “and cut them down in the head, all of them.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 3: ‘David, King (may his memory be blessed), further said: "My fear is within my joy, and my joy is within my fear; and my love ascends above them all. Therefore, the Holy One, blessed be He, made a covenant with me that I should be proficient in the Scripture, in the Mishnah, in the laws, and in the aggadahs, as it is said, 'For is not my house so with God? For He has made an everlasting covenant with me, ordered in all things, and sure; for all my salvation, and all my desire, will He not make it to grow' (2 Samuel 23). And there is no covenant but the Torah, as it is said, 'My covenant was with him, life and peace' (Malachi 2). Ordered in all things, in the Scripture, in the Mishnah, in…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 3) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 3: a life without grief and without the evil inclination, how so, etc.; the distress of Joseph sprang upon him, etc., because he still required further preparation in awe,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For it is a sweetening at the root, transforming bitterness into sweetness, where the fear itself becomes joy, as written in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah (chapter 3): "I rejoiced out of my fear"; and this is possible only within the fear of Hashem, whereas with other fears it merely brings to joy afterward.

As in Tanna Devei Eliyahu (Rabbah 6): Even if a man committed one hundred sins, one greater than the other, and repented, the Holy One says: “Behold, I am with him in mercy” — meaning if a person prays a single prayer from the depth of his heart, all sins between man and God are pardoned immediately.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: With Heaven's help, concerning the title of this holy book which we named with the title becoming it, Ohr Zaru'a LaTzaddik: my friend, the eminent and pious Rabbi Eliezer Tzvi Ziegelman, may his lamp shine, remarked: it is named after the verse, "but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings" [Exodus 10:23], since the first treatise in this holy work discusses the exile and Exodus from Egypt, thus far his words.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Hence the Blessed Name created darkness so that man through his toil should forge light out of darkness; and through Israel restraining their physical desires, they illuminate their souls and achieve clear recognition of their Creator. And this is what is written: “He declared the power of His works to His people, to give them the heritage of nations” — meaning that the Blessed Name revealed to them even the light that transcends their natural grasp—the hidden lights of the six days of creation—so that through Israel's service darkness turns into light.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Psalms 104:23: ‘People then go out to their work,to their labor until the evening.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Psalms 104:23) to illuminate his teaching here (“whereas "man goes forth to his work and to his labor"— meaning his active exertion—"until evening". Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Immediately, each and every one emerged strictly according to its kind; whereupon the Angel of the World opened and exclaimed (Psalms 104:31): “May the glory of the Lord endure forever; let the Lord rejoice in His works.” Behold, we already explained above the distinction between grasses and trees: that grasses are sown anew each time, whereas trees are permanent, planted only once initially, after which the sap rises and nourishes them continually.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Exodus 25:8: ‘And let them make Me a sanctuary that I may dwell among them.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Exodus 25:8) to illuminate his teaching here (“which was necessary preparation for "And let them make Me a sanctuary", is forbidden on Shabbat, for the reality of "and I will dwell in their midst" has already been accomplished. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And so will it be in the future at the final completion of this world. Nevertheless, as a preparation for 'I am', one requires likewise human exertion through mortal power in 'turning away from evil', which is the indispensable preparation for 'doing good'.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 9:4

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Exodus 35:22: ‘Men and women, all whose hearts moved them, all who would make an elevation offering of gold to GOD, came bringing brooches, earrings, rings, and pendants uncertain; cf. Num. 31.50.—gold objects of all kinds.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Exodus 35:22) to illuminate his teaching here (“and therefore "the men came alongside the women" in the construction of the Tabernacle, because woman embodies the fear of Hashem, as is known; and therefore the women brought exclusively gold, alluding to the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Meaning that even in realms beyond human consciousness altogether, there too man is tasked with bringing elevation and rectification. And so we see that an unwitting sin (shogeg) requires atonement—yet surely it is no worse than an act of duress (ones), and the Merciful One exempts one under duress, all the more so an inadvertent act performed without conscious intent!

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Deuteronomy 20:19: ‘When in your war against a city you have to besiege it a long time in order to capture it, you must not destroy its trees, wielding the ax against them. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And there exist multiple distinct arrangements correlating the tribes to the months, each being absolute truth in its own dimension; and the arrangement manifest at their root and crown in Nissan—which is the head of the months whence all expand—is the order of the princes dedicated therein [where Pagiel ben Ochran of Asher offered on the eleventh day, corresponding to Shevat]; for Asher corresponds to Shevat, containing the New Year for Trees (Rosh Hashanah 2a); the vegetative soul (nefesh ha-tzomachat) within man: "for man is as the tree of the field" (Devarim 20:19), which grows, multiplies, and receives influx from the element of water within him.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “Now the serpent was more subtle than any beast of the field...” The matter of the serpent relates to the verse (Deuteronomy 25:11–12): “When men strive together... then you shall cut off her hand,” as explained in Mei HaShiloach (Vol. 1, Bereishit, s.v. Vayomer El HaIsha, and in the marginal notes there). And this sin of Adam HaRishon occurred before he entered the corporeal body of this physical world, as taught in the Zohar (Kedoshim 83b): Primordial Adam had nothing of this physical world; once he sinned he darkened, diminished himself, and required another body, etc..

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 2:9: ‘And from the ground the ETERNAL God caused to grow every tree that was pleasing to the sight and good for food, with the tree of life in the middle of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and bad.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:26, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 2:9) to illuminate his teaching here (“"every tree pleasant to the sight" Genesis 2:9—this is the externality of all his faculties; "and good for food"—this is the inner core; "and the Tree of Life"—this is the heart, as it is written Proverbs 4:23: "for...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And from this flows physical beauty which is perceived strictly through the eyes: "pleasant to the sight" (Bereishis 2:9) and "a delight to the eyes" (ibid. 3:6); a blind man feeling no sensation of beauty, for this perception exists only through the power of sight; wherefore the essence of beauty resides within the eyes: "a bride whose eyes are beautiful requires no examination of her body" (Ta'anit 24a); beautiful eyes testifying to the beauty of the entire body; and bleary eyes testifying to bodily ugliness.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For the entire creation of the cosmos is mirrored within the human soul; and the “shattered worlds” correspond within the soul to the broken heart—over the failure wherein he stumbled, through which he ultimately attains true depth in the words of Torah. And as it is written (Genesis 2:6): “And a mist went up from the earth”—referring to the yearning cry rising from the shattered worlds, as taught in Tikkunei HaZohar (Tikkun 52, 87a): “Ed” represents the letters Aleph-Dalet of the Name Adonai; come and see: an arousal from below to above is required first, and only afterward “and watered the whole face of the ground.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 4:23: ‘More than all that you guard, guard your mind,For it is the source of life.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:26, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 4:23) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written Proverbs 4:23: "for out of it are the issues of life", standing within it, as is known that it is in the center of the body. "And the Tree of Knowledge"—this is the brain, which distinguishes between...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Concerning which Sanhedrin (106b) states: "the Merciful One desires the heart," as it is said: "but Hashem looks on the heart" (I Samuel 16:7), rather than mere brain intellect, for what is in the heart diffuses throughout the entire body, from the heart flowing the issues of life (Proverbs 4:23). Whereas intellectual knowledge in the brain alone remains superficial lip-service, failing to suffuse the body; for behold, Balaam clearly knew the supreme virtue of Israel, yet why did he not join them? Because he knew it in his mind, but not in his heart.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 44:9
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And the membrane of pri'ah corresponds to absorbing light beyond what is proper, and this is not wholly evil; therefore the commandment in this is to peel back and part the membrane to either side, in the manner stated by King Solomon (Proverbs 4:15): “Avoid it (pera'ehu), pass not by it” (and as explained at length in Parashat Vayeira).

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: The essence of the festival of Shavuot is primarily because it is the season of the Giving of our Torah; as established by the Men of the Great Assembly in the liturgy of prayer; who instituted the prayers for Israel, as written in Berachos (33a); and one must wonder at the Magen Avraham (beginning of §494) who wrote: "our custom to recite 'the season of the Giving of our Torah'" is based on the ruling of the Rambam; attributing to "our custom" that which has been universally self-evident unto all Israel across the entire world from time immemorial!

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Not so in coldness and detachment, where study does not pass through the heart: even though he grasps wisdom in his brain and perceives concepts of Godliness and Torah, the heart remains wholly unmoved, as though learning an external science with which he has no personal stake, because fear of sin did not precede to make him reflect on his deficiency and his need for Torah to heal him—and then his wisdom does not endure, as stated of Doeg in Sanhedrin 106b who forgot everything, because the Merciful One desires the heart, that Torah be felt within the heart, which is essential, for then it possesses vitality and is absorbed within him.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And through forcibly grasping bounty beyond what Hashem intended to bestow—along the lines of “Audacity is effective even toward Heaven” (Sanhedrin 105a) — they corrupted the earthly soil below and blemished the supernal Earth at its root, which serves as the garment for the Land of the Living. As in Zohar (Vayigash 205b) on Isaiah 42:5: “He that gives soul unto the people upon it”—Rabbi Yehudah said: all is rooted Above, and this Earth receives the soul to impart unto all.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ecclesiastes 10:2: ‘A sage’s mind tends toward the right hand, a fool’s toward the left.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:26, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Ecclesiastes 10:2) to illuminate his teaching here (“in which dwell the good and evil inclinations: "A wise man's heart, etc.", and they warned: "you shall not wander after your heart"; and desires emanate from the heart, and thus they stumbled through appetites in eating;”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And "If Israel kept two Shabbats they would be redeemed" (Shabbat 118b): one may say this refers to man's primary labor being in concrete action with the limbs through which all commandments and prohibitions of the Torah are fulfilled, and all sins being ascribed to the Nefesh: "if a soul sins" [Leviticus 5:1], for sin occurs in action where in the world of Asiyah evil dominates as is known; and likewise in the emotional traits of the heart where the Ruach dwells in Yetzirah, where good and evil are balanced as is known, for there is the abode of the two inclinations: "a wise man's heart is at his right, but a fool's heart at his left" [Ecclesiastes 10:2]…

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And so too, what Avraham our Father was 'serving' toward the sun in his early days, he was not worshipping the physical sunlight; rather to the celestial song he perceived, how the sun glorifies Hashem, which is a channeled force from Hashem—toward that was his devotion directed. And this is what is brought in the holy Zohar (Balak 201b): “A Psalm: Sing unto Hashem a new song, etc., His right hand has wrought salvation for Him,” wrought salvation for whom? For this very Psalm, etc.”.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Numbers 15:39: ‘That shall be your fringe; look at it and recall all GOD’s commandments and observe them, so that you do not follow your heart and eyes in your urge to stray.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:26, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Numbers 15:39) to illuminate his teaching here (“and they warned: "you shall not wander after your heart"; and desires emanate from the heart, and thus they stumbled through appetites in eating; and therefore the woman stumbled who is filled with yearning,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And as written: "and you shall look upon it and remember, etc., and that you seek not after your own heart and your own eyes after which you go astray"— an expression of straying/fornication; and specifically "you", indicating that temptation is common among you. And as written in chapter HeChalil (Sukkah 52a): on the verse "for he has magnified to do great things"— that the inclination bypasses the nations and incites against Israel, and whoever is greater, his inclination is greater.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 55:15
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: To lean passively upon the spiritual refinement that exists without action on their part; rather, all the days that they live upon the face of the earth they contract themselves and engage in Torah and practical commandments, to clarify and illuminate before the eyes of all why Hashem chose them alone. And concerning this it is stated (Proverbs 15:19): “The way of the sluggard is as a hedge of thorns; but the path of the upright is made a highway”, and as brought on this in Mei HaShiloach (Part I, Parashat Bo) on the verse “Draw out and take you lambs”.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 3:16: ‘And to the woman [God] said,“I will greatly expandYour toil—and your pregnancies;In hardship shall you bear children.Yet your urge shall be for your husband,And his will shall prevail over yours.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:26, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 3:16) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written Genesis 3:16: "and your desire shall be to your husband", and through the serpent who was full of lust, as written in Shabbat 110a: "a woman in whom a serpent has nested", and as I wrote elsewhere.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Yet when Hashem asked the woman: “What is this that you have done?” and she said: “The serpent beguiled me”—this was no valid claim at all; Adam’s claim was grounded, for being part of him he could not sever himself from her; but the woman should have distanced herself from the serpent and severed all connection from him.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: The explanation of this is found in Shabbat (63b) on Ecclesiastes 11:9: “Rejoice, O young man, in your youth... but know that for all these God will bring you into judgment”—up to here for words of Torah, from here onward for good deeds. Meaning, words of Torah, being pure and clear, one may pursue in vast expanse; but mitzvot and good deeds, executed through corporeal bodily actions, require rigorous calculation and deep purification.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Isaiah 58:11: ‘GOD will guide you always—Slaking your thirst in parched places And giving strength to your bones.You shall be like a watered garden,Like a spring whose waters do not fail.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:26, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Isaiah 58:11) to illuminate his teaching here (“because it terminates, in the sense of "whose waters fail/deceive", is termed dead, meaning: it is severed and absent, lacking the Aleph from Emet leaving Met - dead,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Thus physical matter is the true illusion, "falsehood" denoting that which lacks permanence: "The lip of truth shall be established forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment" [Proverbs 12:19]; "falsehood" (kazav) meaning something that terminates, as in "whose waters fail not (lo yechazvu)" [Isaiah 58:11]. Wherefore worldly passions are termed "falsehood": "Bread of deceit (shaker) is sweet to a man" [Proverbs 20:17] [and note the precision of the Holy Tongue: the matriarch of lust in the desert was named Cozbi (Kozbi), signifying deception].
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “These are the generations of Noah, etc.” It is written (Isaiah 58:13–14): “If you restrain your foot because of the Sabbath, from pursuing your affairs on My holy day, and call the Sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord honorable, and honor it, not going your own ways, nor seeking your own pleasure, nor speaking a word; then shall you delight yourself in the Lord, and I will make you ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Taanit 5b: ‘Rabbi Yitzḥak said to Rav Naḥman that Rabbi Yoḥanan said as follows: Old age sprang upon Samuel, which caused him to appear older than his actual age, as it is written: “I regret that I made Saul king” (I Samuel 15:11). Samuel said before God: Master of the Universe, You have considered me the equivalent of Moses and Aaron, as it is written: “Moses and Aaron among His priests, and Samuel among those who call upon His Name” (Psalms 99:6). Just as with regard to Moses and Aaron, their handiwork was not annulled in their lifetimes, so too, let my handiwork not be annulled in my lifetime. I anointed Saul; please do not annul his reign.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:26, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Taanit 5b) to illuminate his teaching here (“our Sages of blessed memory said of him Ta'anit 5b: that he did not die.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Thus classical prophecy operates on the principle that "one person is pushed aside for another," others being lowered so that one may rise. And this explains the early death of Samuel the Ramathite because he was pushed aside for Saul (Ta'anit 5b), of which it is said: "I have hewed them by the prophets..." [Hosea 6:5], bringing this vulnerability upon himself by instituting this dynamic.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this clarifies the Midrash that on the third day the work of the waters was completed: namely, from that which was said on the third day, “Let the waters gather... and let the dry land appear, and it was so,” which indicates that space is made available for whoever desires to recognize His divine glory; this itself proves that at the root they are entirely one with the upper waters with no distinction at all.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 18:16: ‘A gift eases a person’s wayAnd gives access to the great.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 18:16) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written Proverbs 18:16: "A man's gift makes room for him, etc.". Facing him is the river Pishon— an expression of expansion and abundance, like the attribute of Chesed which expands and abounds.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: The delight he then experiences cannot be compared to the delight of one who was never exiled and never tasted poverty at all. Similar teachings appear in the Midrash and the Zohar, as is known. This is the sanctity of Rosh Chodesh: the renewal of the moon's light after it has darkened. It was given to Israel, who are destined to renew themselves like the moon.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 12:7 (§2)
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Akin to what is brought in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 44a): “'The rich answers roughly' (Proverbs 18:23)—this is Joshua,” namely when he battled against Ai and did not succeed the first time, he then pleaded: “And what will You do for Your great Name?” (Joshua 7:9), since You had already begun delivering beforehand and Israel grew mighty, and now if You abandon them, there will be a desecration of Hashem's Name in this.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ecclesiastes 5:9: ‘A lover of money is never satisfied with money, nor a lover of wealth, with income. That too is futile.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Ecclesiastes 5:9) to illuminate his teaching here (“as in Ecclesiastes 5:9 "He that loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver", he who has a hundred desires two hundred, etc. And so our Sages said Sukkah 52b: he who sates it leaves it hungrier; and likewise they...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: But he who is "a lover of silver shall not be satisfied with silver" (Koheles 5:9), for the lust of the burning yetzer is boundless; for this is the entire strategy of the yetzer: seeking to capture the boundless yearning planted in the human heart; which is the holy yearning of the yetzer tov for Torah and divine service transcending the world of limits; this being the heritage of Jacob without boundaries (Shabbat 118b); meaning his portion in the supernal Land, the World to Come where boundaries do not exist.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And God said, Let there be light.” It is written (Zechariah 14:6): “And it shall come to pass on that day, that there shall not be light, but heavy clouds and thick darkness (yekarot ve-kipaon)”; and the Gemara expounds upon this (Pesachim 50a): “This refers to the light that is precious (yakar) in this world, but commonplace/solidified (kafui) in the World to Come.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sukkah 52b: ‘Rav Ḥana bar Aḥa said that the Sages in the school of Rav say: There are four creations that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created, yet He, as it were, regrets that He created them, as they do more harm than good. And these are they: Exile, Chaldeans, and Ishmaelites, and the evil inclination. Exile, as it is written: “Now therefore, for what am I here, says the Lord, seeing that My people is taken away for naught” (Isaiah 52:5). God Himself is asking: For what am I here? Chaldeans, as it is written: “Behold the land of the Chaldeans, this is the people that was not” (Isaiah 23:13), meaning, if only they never were.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Sukkah 52b) to illuminate his teaching here (“And so our Sages said Sukkah 52b: he who sates it leaves it hungrier; and likewise they expounded in the realm of holiness regarding "He that loves silver". And Pishon is the Nile of Egypt, the nakedness of the earth,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Misleading him to believe the trial was whether he would forfeit both worlds by disobeying God's command to preserve Isaac and Israel's destiny. And this was Abraham's great trial: the inclination inverting the perspective, arguing the test was the opposite; except that there an element of natural love was involved in sparing Isaac, wherefore Abraham suspected himself that fatherly love was deceiving him into calling evil good.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And likewise within Klal Yisrael, every individual soul has a specific mitzvah uniquely aligned with his spiritual portion, in which he must exert himself above all to achieve refinement, as stated (Shabbat 118b): “With which mitzvah was your father especially careful? With tzitzit”—and by this one person is distinguished from another in spiritual station.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 40:4: ‘“It was when he drew near to come to Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife: Behold, I know now that you are a woman of fair appearance” (Genesis 12:11). “It will be, when the Egyptians will see you, they will say: This is his wife, and they will kill me, and keep you alive” (Genesis 12:12). “Please, say you are my sister, so that it may be well with me because of you, and my soul shall live because of you” (Genesis 12:13). “It was when he drew near to come to Egypt” – he was together with her all those years, and only now he says to her: “Behold, I know now that you are a woman of fair appearance”? The explanation is that due to travel a person [usually] becomes unsightly, but this one…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 40:4) to illuminate his teaching here (“as our Sages of blessed memory noted Bereishit Rabbah 40:4 regarding Sarah, for Egypt was the epicenter of illicit desires. And this is what is written in the Zohar Lech Lecha 81b: regarding "And Abram went down into...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 7:12 (§2)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Two categories of pedigree: guarding the covenant of circumcision (shemirat habrit), physical lineage visible to all; yet even here a root bearing gall may corrupt, as Esau from Isaac. Slander being a symptom of flawed inner pedigree. While guarding the tongue attests to essential spiritual pedigree, even if lacking hereditary nobility.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Even though human self-restraint is on a lowly plane and of minute scale, as written: “this day upon your heart,” expounded in Mei HaShiloach regarding the Men of Jericho (Pesachim 56a): today the mitzvot rest externally “upon your heart,” while in the World to Come they will be ingrained internally “within your heart.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Zohar, Lech Lecha 11:102-12:113: ‘AND ABRAM WENT DOWN TO EGYPT TO SOJOURN THERE. Why to Egypt? Because it is compared to the Garden of the Lord, as it is written, “Like the garden of the Lord, like the land of Egypt”. For there a certain stream (from the Garden) which is on the right descends and flows, as it is written, “The name of the one was Pishon, that it is which compasseth the whole land of Havilah where there is gold” (Gen. 2, 11).’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Lech Lecha 11:102-12:113) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this is what is written in the Zohar Lech Lecha 81b: regarding "And Abram went down into Egypt, etc.", the river that flows to the right, as it is written: "The name of the first is Pishon, etc.".”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud:7 (§13)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And also because the core realization innovated for Joseph then— was this mystery: that there is a descent which is solely for the sake of ascent; for the spiritual level of Joseph the Righteous was completely fenced in discipline, being fundamentally righteous, having never committed a sin; whereas regarding Judah it is stated: 'And Judah went down' (Genesis 38:1), for King David, peace be upon him, established the yoke of repentance, in the realm of 'where penitents stand, etc.' (Berakhot 34b).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 31:10–11
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And Avraham our Father was in this world just as the soul is within the body, for he is called in the holy Zohar (Lech Lecha 79b): “the Soul of the soul”, and he illuminated to the whole world that Hashem's glory fills all, and through him began perfection for the soul in this physical world. And behold, Avraham who corresponds to the Soul began ascending above this world, which is compared to the body, rising and descending.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 2:11: ‘The name of the first is Pishon, the one that winds through the whole land of Havilah, where the gold is.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 2:11) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written: "The name of the first is Pishon, etc.". "Good for food" corresponds to Isaac, for the attribute of Judgment is not pleasant to the eye, yet it is good for nourishment,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this spiritual acquisition is gathered in exile, wherein the Jewish people absorb the particular power of each land— the obstinacy and 'heart of stone' characteristic of each culture. And by demonstrating that in that very domain they are not blind, obstinate captives, but can bend and sanctify it toward Heaven's glory according to Hashem's will— through this occurs the mystical gathering of converts, wherein even the stone-hearted resolve of the nations is harmonized into Israel and sanctified in their name.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And why at the dawn of creation the Name Elohim alone is mentioned, whereas later when the sprouts stood poised at the threshold of the soil it states (Genesis 2:5): “For the Lord God (Havayah Elohim) had not caused it to rain” — the reason is that Elohim represents strict judgment and structural causality; and when Hashem willed to emanate the world He set up a prime cause—the Name Elohim, meaning “Master of all powers”— through which all worlds cascaded by strict cause and effect.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Pirkei Avot 4:1: ‘Ben Zoma said: Who is wise? He who learns from every man, as it is said: “From all who taught me have I gained understanding” (Psalms 119:99). Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: “He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city” (Proverbs 16:32). Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot, as it is said: “You shall enjoy the fruit of your labors, you shall be happy and you shall prosper” (Psalms 128:2) “You shall be happy” in this world, “and you shall prosper” in the world to come. Who is he that is honored? He who honors his fellow human beings as it is said: “For I honor those that honor Me, but…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Pirkei Avot 4:1) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written Avot 4:1: "Who is mighty? He that subdues his inclination". And facing him is Gihon, which bursts forth with ferocious strength, as it is written Proverbs 19:12: "The king's wrath is as the roaring...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And Torah is the antidote-spice against the evil inclination, as our Sages taught in Bava Batra (16a), Sukkah (52b), and Kiddushin (30b). And likewise they said: "Who is mighty?" [the rung of Isaac's Gevurah]—"He who subdues his inclination" (Avot 4:1). And the Land of Israel is the direct antithesis of subjugation to the foreign empires.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Wherefore justice dictates that in the future Hashem will restore all forbidden realms as holy acquisitions, fulfilling: “The Lord looses the prisoners (matir asurim)”—permitting the forbidden (matir issurim); for issur denotes that man is bound and constrained from absorbing that realm, and through negative commandments he secures eternal treasure.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 19:12: ‘The rage of a king is like the roar of a lion;His favor is like dew upon the grass.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 19:12) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written Proverbs 19:12: "The king's wrath is as the roaring of a lion", which "compasses the whole land of Cush" Genesis 2:13— for the Ethiopians/Cushites are not outwardly pleasing in complexion so I heard...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Meaning the primary source of all manners of immersion in evil, which is the heritage of the nations and not the portion of Israel at all. For the essential root of Israel is like a flock of sheep following after their Shepherd, possessing no immersion in any mundane entity, but drawn purely after the will of the Blessed Name Who guides them; except that through the "yeast in the dough" [the yetzer hara] seductions and incitements of the evil heritage of the nations enter the heart through the mixture of good and evil wrought by sin, which automatically causes the subjugation to the kingdoms of the world.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this corresponds to Proverbs 19:17: “He who is gracious to the poor lends unto the Lord”; the meaning being: man might fear giving to the poor lest harm result, the recipient using that vitality to commit sin, making the giver an accomplice to transgressors; therefore Scripture affirms: “He who is gracious to the poor lends unto the Lord” — meaning that man must perform this act of giving with courageous trust in Hashem that He will guide it along paths of truth so that no ruin results from this bestowal.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 2:13: ‘The name of the second river is Gihon, the one that winds through the whole land of Cush.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 2:13) to illuminate his teaching here (“which "compasses the whole land of Cush" Genesis 2:13— for the Ethiopians/Cushites are not outwardly pleasing in complexion so I heard as well. The Tree of Knowledge of good and evil—”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And therefore it encompasses even the broken vessels as mentioned above. Yet it remains concealed, and it is impossible to gaze at the Surrounding Light through the vessels of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, since the broken vessels interpose between them, unless one ascends directly through them; and there stumbled Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, and Acher (Elisha ben Abuyah).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And likewise it is said concerning Adam HaRishon (Genesis 2:25): “And they were both naked... and were not ashamed,” which Targum Yonatan renders: “and they did not wait for their glory.” Therefore the Blessed Name declared henceforth: “This is the token of the covenant, etc.,” commanding that this bold certainty be concealed and cloaked, so as never to grasp the light stripped of garments.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Isaiah 30:21: ‘and, whenever you deviate to the right or to the left, your ears will heed the command from behind you: “This is the road; follow it!”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Isaiah 30:21) to illuminate his teaching here (“"This is the way, etc.", and from it practical guidance emanated into the world and Jacob also embodies the sefirah of Da'at, as written in the Zohar: Moses within is Jacob without.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this reflects what is stated: 'and your eyes shall see your Teacher' (Isaiah 30:20), which means that whatever a person beholds, he learns from it some lesson for the service of Hashem, for surely not in vain was this sight shown to him from Heaven, rather so that he derive from it a path in the service of Hashem; and likewise whatever he hears, he learns from it for paths of divine service, in the manner stated: 'And your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying: This is the way, walk in it' (Isaiah 30:21).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 45:5
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “To perfect the world under the sovereignty of the Almighty”— meaning that this Name be rectified in wholeness so that concealment no longer exists in the world, and “your Teacher shall not hide Himself anymore” (Isaiah 30:20); and then Hashem's light will shine upon all recorded for life, and the four-letter Name Havayah will be unveiled: “And Hashem shall be King over all the earth; in that day shall Hashem be One, and His Name One” (Zechariah 14:9), and in us will be fulfilled the scripture that is written (Isaiah 25:9).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 3:5: ‘but God knows that as soon as you eat of it your eyes will be opened and you will be like divine beings who know good and bad.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 3:5) to illuminate his teaching here (“"and you shall be as gods"—creators of worlds; for such indeed is the power of one cleaving to truth and to the Torah of truth, as it is written Sanhedrin 65b: "If the righteous desired, they could create a world"....”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Rather than deriving sustenance from that which contravenes the will of the Blessed Name; which was the secret of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil where the Serpent seduced them: "Then your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be as gods" (Bereishis 3:5); thinking they would no longer depend upon divine governance or remain subjugated unto Him, but could govern themselves independently according to their own will.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: So here it will be clarified that the syntax joins with what precedes, Hashem having entrusted the matter to human clarification. And indeed we see that the Holy One did not state definitively that Adam ate what was forbidden, asking him only interrogatively: “Have you eaten of the tree whereof I commanded you not to eat?” — proving that the reality hangs on man's clarification, whereby it may emerge that he ate only the good and not the evil.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sanhedrin 65b: ‘Rava says: If the righteous wish to do so, they can create a world, as it is stated: “But your iniquities have separated between you and your God.” In other words, there is no distinction between God and a righteous person who has no sins, and just as God created the world, so can the righteous. Indeed, Rava created a man, a golem, using forces of sanctity. Rava sent his creation before Rabbi Zeira. Rabbi Zeira would speak to him but he would not reply. Rabbi Zeira said to him: You were created by one of the members of the group, one of the Sages. Return to your dust.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 65b) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written Sanhedrin 65b: "If the righteous desired, they could create a world". Only the physical eating of it was prohibited, just as the vocal pronunciation of the Ineffable Name is forbidden Havayah is the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: However, in truth the power of the part mirrors the power of the whole, and just as "by the word of Hashem the heavens were made", so our Sages said (Sanhedrin 65b): "If the righteous so desired, they could create a world," and those who occupied themselves with Sefer Yetzirah and created, etc. For the Covenant of the Tongue corresponds to the Covenant of Circumcision (Ma'or), only that circumcision represents the 'Lower Union', namely the power of actualization into practical deed, which is the union of masculine and feminine.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 11:9–10
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And just as there is a difference between weekdays and Yom Tov, so there is a distinction between the sanctity of Yom Tov and that of Shabbat: the sanctity of Yom Tov is that Israel sanctifies it, while the sanctity of Shabbat is inherently fixed, an acceptable time and the Will of all wills. And this was the spiritual path of Avraham our Father, peace be upon him, who refused to expand into worldly pursuits like the people of his generation, and even within holy matters Hashem bestowed upon him he did not expand complacently.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 5: ‘[Laws Regarding The Proper] Intent [When Reciting] The Blessings. Containing 1 Se'if:One should have in mind the meaning of the words when reciting blessings. When articulating the Name , one should have in mind the meaning of the Name as it is pronounced - Adon-ai : that He is Lord over all. And one should have in mind [the meaning of the Name] as it is spelled with a Yud-Hei that He Was , Is , and Will Be . And when articulating the Name Elo-him , have in mind that He is Strong, Omnipotent, and Master of all powers.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this commentary and philosophical-halakhic exposition (Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 5) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in the Tur, Orach Chayyim, section 5, and likewise "truth" as written in the Yerushalmi at the beginning of Sanhedrin, and likewise the heritage of Jacob is without boundaries,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For the Name Havayah denotes the Holy One, Blessed be He, in His infinite expansion far above our finite human comprehension; likewise, the Name Havayah denotes "He was, He is, and He will be," as codified in the Tur, Orach Chaim (siman 5), which embodies an endless, eternal expansion concealed from our temporal perception, as taught in Tractate Pesachim (50a): "'This is My Name forever (l'olam / l'alem — to be hidden),' etc.," meaning that in this world it is not pronounced as written, because its transcendent reality cannot be grasped at all.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Balak 8
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And he looked on the Kenites, and he took up his parable and said, your dwelling place is strong, and you put your nest [ken] in a rock.” (Bamidbar, 24:21)Meaning that from him a Parsha was carved (as in a rock) in the words of Torah, and the words of Torah are living and enduring forever (“your dwelling place is strong”).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 118b: ‘Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: One who delights in Shabbat is rescued from the oppression of exile. He derives it by means of a verbal analogy. It is written here, with regard to Shabbat: “And I will cause you to ride on the heights [bamotei] of the world” (Isaiah 58:14), and it is written there: “You are fortunate Israel, who is like you? A nation redeemed by God, the shield that aids you and the sword of your triumph. Your enemies will try to defeat you and you will trample their high places [bamoteimo]” (Deuteronomy 33:29). Rav Yehuda said that Rav said: With regard to anyone who delights in the Shabbat, God grants him his heart’s desires, as it is stated: “And you shall delight in God…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 118b) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in Shabbat 118b, meaning that it has no finite border, and as written Proverbs 12:19: "The lip of truth shall be established forever, etc." to utter it with its letters in this world”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: He will nonetheless have tranquility because he recognizes that it is from Hashem, blessed be He, and is for the good. But in Israel it is the reverse: every punishment is only “to the outward eye,” in this world; and even one upon whom, God forbid, “cutting off of children” was decreed — that is only in this world, but their souls are “bound in the bond of life” and rise for the resurrection of the dead and for Olam Haba.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: The test of this is found in Berakhot (4a) regarding David's claim: "Am I not pious?": as explained above (folio 8a) that David demonstrated total purity from the three master vices: envy, lust, and honor, see there.
