Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Psalms 119:126: ‘It is a time to act for GOD,for they have violated Your teaching.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:34, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Psalms 119:126) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written Psalms 119:126: “It is time to act for Hashem, they have made void Your Torah”, and when evil seeks to hijack the Right, as they taught in Berakhot 61a: the evil inclination sits at the two valves of...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And through this there is sometimes “a time to act for Hashem — they have voided Your Torah” (Tehillim 119:126) — they have made void Your Torah.” The Sages read the verse in both directions and invoked it to sanction committing the Oral Torah to writing — “a time to act for Hashem” overriding the rule that oral teachings not be set down (Gittin 60a; Temurah 14b; and see Berachos 63a).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And the earth was unformed (tohu) and void (bohu).” It is stated (in Sefer HaBahir, §2): “Tohu is something that confounds/misleads human beings; Bohu means ‘it is in it’ (bo hu).” The meaning of this is: when Hashem shows a person that He validates and grants space to his divine service, the person must then serve Hashem with even greater humility and must not assume personal pride or assertiveness simply because Hashem revealed that his toil holds significance.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 61a: ‘Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak strongly objects to this: If that is so that you understand the verse literally, what do you say about the verse with regard to Elkana, the father of the prophet Samuel, as it is written: “And Elkana walked after his wife,” and what of the verse with regard to the prophet Elisha, as it is written: “And he arose and followed her” (II Kings 4:30)? Here, too, then the verse concerning Manoah may be similarly interpreted; he followed his wife’s words and followed her advice, and did not literally walk behind her.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:34, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 61a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as they taught in Berakhot 61a: the evil inclination sits at the two valves of the heart, even upon the right and the good— one must sometimes proceed to the left and break the baseline words of Torah”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And then they derive delight from the radiance of the Shechinah—namely Ruach HaKodesh, which arrives through this into the wisdom of the kidneys [as our Sages stated (Berakhot 61a): "the kidneys give counsel"; and regarding one who studies Torah for its own sake: "people derive from him counsel and sound wisdom" (Avot 6:1); and lishmah is feminine, known from the Ari to mean for the sake of the Name of the Shechinah; and this is not the place to elaborate], which become like two gushing springs, and a living spring has no cessation, limit, or boundary whatsoever.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And if a person totally entrusts his soul to Hashem before sleep, then even during sleep when he is devoid of consciousness, Hashem testifies that he remains cleaving to Him. As taught in the Gemara (Berakhot 35a): “Here before a blessing, there after a blessing”—reciting a blessing beforehand unites with the One, while eating without a blessing turns Dalet into Reish.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 123b: ‘Rava said to him: After all, it was taught in the Tosefta: They permitted, what difference is there to me if it is for the purpose of utilizing the object itself, and what difference is there to me if it is for the purpose of utilizing its place; why introduce distinctions that are not explicitly stated in the Tosefta? Rather, Rava said that it should be explained as follows: Initially, they permitted moving an object whose primary function is for a permitted use, both for the purpose of utilizing the object itself and for the purpose of sitting in or utilizing its place. And then they permitted moving that object from the sun into the shade. And then they permitted moving an object…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:34, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 123b) to illuminate his teaching here (“and as I heard regarding “rinsing the entrails overrides the Sabbath”. And as our Sages of blessed memory stated Yevamot 90b: in all matters if a prophet tells you to temporarily violate Torah, obey him, provided he...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And Nechemyah went beyond them, making a safeguard for the need of the hour, even one not fit to endure forever — for with muktzeh they permitted, then re-forbade, as they said [Shabbos 123b], “in the days of Nechemyah ben Chachalyah this mishnah was taught” — all according to what he saw was needed to fence in the generation, that they not return to folly.], as it is written, ‘in those days I saw in Yehudah men treading winepresses on Shabbos’ (Nechemyah 13:15)” — the muktzeh restrictions were tightened, later relaxed, then re-tightened, per the generation’s need. R’ Tzadok: Nechemyah pioneered even temporary fences for the hour.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And regarding what the holy Ari writes in Sha'ar HaHakdamot (32b) that prior to rectification love did not exist between the sefirot, but only the attribute of fear — whereas according to our explanation the primary rectification was to introduce awe among the sefirot as the vessel to contain the light so it would not flee to its source, which they lacked, while love they possessed abundantly, yearning passionately to return to their source — indeed, this is reconciled as follows: they possessed fear, but not true, rectified awe.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Pesachim 65b: ‘MISHNA: These are the matters related to the Paschal lamb that override Shabbat, when the eve of Passover occurs on Shabbat: Its slaughter, the sprinkling of its blood, the cleaning of its intestines and the burning of its fats on the altar, all of which are services that must be performed on Passover eve while it is still day. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is “with all your heart” — meaning even amid the loves and desires of this world; “and with all your soul” is in the manner brought [Berachos 63a], “‘in all your ways know Him’ — even in a matter of transgression,” the intent being like the aveirah lishmah mentioned.].” R’ Tzadok ties this to aveirah lishmah — serving God “with all your soul” even along paths that appear forbidden, when done purely for His sake.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As it is written: “A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day”; Shabbat indicates that all of creation is still held within His blessed hand and not yet severed in autonomous self-awareness, unable as yet to gaze or exist as an independent entity on its own, and as it is taught in the Gemara (Chagigah 13b): “Chashmal — at times silent (chashot), and at times speaking (memalelot)”; at the moment when the divine speech emanates from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, they are silent and hold no independent power because they are still submerged within His blessed hand, and likewise on every Sabbath creation returns to be re-absorbed into its Source.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yevamot 90b: ‘The Gemara suggests: Come and hear another proof. The verse states with regard to a true prophet: “To him you shall listen” (Deuteronomy 18:15). From here it is derived that even if the prophet says to you: Transgress one of the mitzvot of the Torah, for example, as in the case of Elijah at Mount Carmel, who brought an offering to God on that mountain during a period when it was forbidden on pain of karet to sacrifice offerings outside the Temple, with regard to everything that he permits for the requirement of the hour, you must listen to him. This indicates that a Torah mitzva can indeed be uprooted in an active manner.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:34, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Yevamot 90b) to illuminate his teaching here (“And as our Sages of blessed memory stated Yevamot 90b: in all matters if a prophet tells you to temporarily violate Torah, obey him, provided he is like Elijah at Mount Carmel, who is established as a true prophet...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And though for a prophet there is a limit — that “in everything, if he says to transgress the words of Torah, listen to him, except for idolatry” — that [license] is only “by [the word of] a prophet”; but nonetheless, even for a Jew’s sin of idolatry there is a rectification, to be reckoned after teshuvah as “a transgression for its own sake” — for we find an example even in idolatry of “a transgression for its own sake” [Sanhedrin 107a] on the verse “unto the top [rosh]” (II Shmuel 15:32), that “David sought [to serve idolatry]” — see there.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: From which derives temporary active power for every person to expand and assert his might in the world to the utmost, free choice being granted to human sight — therefore they were content to expand during that entire temporal window, unconcerned with securing their existence for eternal life. And even though they clearly knew that when the Blessed Name elevated His attributes above human reach they would inevitably dissolve, nevertheless they were willing to live merely for the transient hour, indulging as they wished in the willful desires of their hearts and dissolving at the end.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 13:11: ‘So Lot chose for himself the whole plain of the Jordan, and Lot journeyed eastward. Thus they parted from each other;’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:34, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 13:11) to illuminate his teaching here (“And the complete separation, “a man from his brother”, arrived specifically after this declaration of “if you take the right, I will go left”, as it is written Proverbs 3:6: “In all your ways acknowledge Him”, and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: But refers to Esau's sons, nephews being termed brothers: "for we are brethren" (Bereishis 13:8); servitude not being mentioned in Jacob's blessing regarding brethren but regarding nations, and Esau's descendants became gentile nations without any link to Israel. But in Isaac's blessing directly unto Esau he declared: "and you shall serve your brother" (Bereishis 27:40); innovating in this blessing that Esau personally must serve Jacob; this alone being the authentic blessing for him, Isaac sensing Esau was unworthy of independent blessing.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And God said, Let there be light.” “Light” is mentioned here five times, signifying five ascending rungs from the moment a person begins engaging in the study and practice of Torah until he arrives at complete spiritual perfection: First: that man consciously recognizes that the Blessed Name is the sole Ruler and Overseer of all existence; Second: that he actively turns his whole being and attention toward the Blessed Name; Third: that the Blessed Name illuminates for man that He Himself derives no personal benefit from human service.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 3:6: ‘In all your ways acknowledge [God],And your paths will be made smooth.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:34, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 3:6) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written Proverbs 3:6: “In all your ways acknowledge Him”, and our Sages of blessed memory expounded in Berakhot 63a: “even in the midst of a transgression”. Then: “and He shall direct your paths”—”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: But even "your paths" where you have already transgressed and strayed off to the side, outside the proper way—if you now fulfill "acknowledge Him," you will realize that this too was encompassed by the Blessed Name, and if so, it is made straight.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” This is what Scripture states (Proverbs 3:19–20): “The Lord by wisdom founded the earth; He established the heavens by understanding; by His knowledge the depths were broken open.” “Earth” corresponds to the human heart, as stated in the Holy Zohar (Tzav 28b), and it signifies the diverse feelings of reverent awe that reside in the heart throughout all the specific details of one's actions; and the awe that is present within the heart sprouts from Chochmah (Wisdom) and a transcendent realm.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 63a: ‘Ḥizkiya, son of Rabbi Parnakh, said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Why is the portion of sota juxtaposed with the portion of terumot and tithes (Numbers ch. 5)? They are juxtaposed to tell you: Anyone who has terumot and tithes and does not give them to a priest, will ultimately require the services of a priest by means of his wife, as it is stated: “And every man’s hallowed things shall be his” (Numbers 5:10). This refers to one who keeps those hallowed items for himself. To this the Torah juxtaposed: “If any man’s wife go aside and act unfaithfully against him” (Numbers 5:12). And it is written: “Then shall the man bring his wife unto the priest” (Numbers 5:15). Moreover, ultimately that man…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:34, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 63a) to illuminate his teaching here (“and our Sages of blessed memory expounded in Berakhot 63a: “even in the midst of a transgression”. Then: “and He shall direct your paths”— meaning: that one surrender himself totally unto Hashem, blessed be He,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Sanctification of the New Moon is the first commandment given to Israel in Egypt, and it was not spoken directly to them, but only to Moses and Aaron, and He did not state that they should say this to all Israel; nonetheless, 'This month shall be unto you'— means unto the whole of Israel, and as stated in the Midrash Rabbah (Shemot, Parashah 15): 'The New Moon is unto you, etc.'
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And God said, Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place.” It is stated in Midrash Rabbah (Bo 15:22) and Tanchuma (Chayei Sarah 3): “‘Unto one place’—this refers to the place of the Leviathan.” The explanation of this is that Leviathan represents the root of continuous, unbroken supernal union; as taught in the Holy Zohar (Vayikra 4a): “Rabbi Elazar asked him: Who are those above and who are those below? He replied: A worthy question; the supernal realm where they abide in joy and oneness, never parting eternally, are termed ‘companions’ (re'im).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 24:1: ‘Abraham was now old, advanced in years, and GOD had blessed Abraham in all things.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:34, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 24:1) to illuminate his teaching here (““And Hashem had blessed Abraham in all things”, and our Sages expounded Bereishit Rabbah 59:7: that he achieved total mastery over his inclination.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Unlike Abraham and Isaac from whom dross emerged, their completeness established only through Jacob's holiness concealed within them; Abraham constantly walking toward the South (negbah), striving to become "dried out" (menugav) of all worldly lusts; while Isaac was already "dwelling in the land of the South" (Bereishis 24:62), his yetzer tamed, needing no warfare against temptation.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this accords with the Holy Zohar (Bereishit 24b) that the entire universe is structured like the concentric layers of an onion—that is, garments— where each successive generation serves as an outer garment to the generation following it, and each later generation possesses a deeper inward vitality. For just as in the body the physical hand and foot are garments for the inner hand and foot of the soul, which act through words of Torah— one receiving Torah wisdom and the other bestowing it upon another—so every generation is a garment for the one that succeeds it.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 59:7: ‘“The Lord blessed Abraham with everything” – Rabbi Yudan and Rabbi Neḥemya, Rabbi Yudan said: [This means] that He granted him a female child. Rabbi Neḥemya said to him: [Even] regarding the primary member of the king’s household, blessing is not written. Rather, “the Lord blessed Abraham with everything” means that He did not grant him a daughter at all. Rabbi Levi said three interpretations: “With everything” means that he granted him control over his evil inclination; “with everything” means that Ishmael repented during his lifetime; “with everything” means that his food storehouse lacked nothing. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Evil detests the good and harbors no desire to cling to it, as stated (Bereishit Rabbah 59): "The cursed does not cling to the blessed"—phrased not as the blessed refusing, but the cursed being unwilling; and though Eliezer desired Isaac for his daughter, it was because he was destined to transition from cursed to blessed (Bereishit Rabbah 60 on "Come in, you blessed of Hashem"); hinting subtly at it with "perhaps (ulai) the woman will not follow," his full transformation awaiting Rebekah's appearance.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Rabbi Chiyya said: Because on them constructive labor is permitted, hence they are not called holy; and regarding this the Sages established the Havdalah blessing dividing between holy and secular. And through man guarding the Sabbath day, never trespassing its borders nor performing mundane labor, he is subsequently enabled during the following six workdays to acquire the blessings of this world with abundant holiness.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 13:14: ‘And GOD said to Abram, after Lot had parted from him, “Raise your eyes and look out from where you are, to the north and south, to the east and west,’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:35, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 13:14) to illuminate his teaching here (“Genesis 13:14 “After Lot had separated from him: Lift up your eyes, please”, for the Land of Israel vomits out sexual immorality, as it is written in Parashat Acharei Mot Leviticus 18:27–28: “For all these...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is the “purpose of ‘the eye sees and the heart covets’” for the Children of Israel — as the Sages said, “what is the desire of Israel? — the Holy One [Himself].” And “the fear of Heaven nullifies all the fears of this world,” and “it draws after it love and pleasure.” — the Jew’s eye, unlike Bilaam’s or Bar Sheishach’s, finds no lasting delight in the body at all; its one true pleasure is to look upward and see the Creator, so that the very faculty of desire is converted into the faculty of fear — and fear draws love in its train, whose object is God Himself.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this corresponds to Deuteronomy 4:19: “And lest you lift up your eyes to heaven”—meaning that you should definitively assert: “This finite form is the ultimate divine Will”—do not say so; for even within the most exalted acts of service and prostration, we cannot declare that they constitute the final essence of God’s absolute Will, because each is merely a temporal garment instituted by Hashem, indicating: “At this moment My Will is manifested in this”.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Leviticus 18:27-28: ‘for all those abhorrent things were done by the people who were in the land before you, and the land became defiled.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:35, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Leviticus 18:27-28) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written in Parashat Acharei Mot Leviticus 18:27–28: “For all these abominations did the men of the land... lest the land vomit you out”; for “the air of the Land of Israel makes one wise” Bava Batra 158b,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 1:1 (§4)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the crucible preparing them for this was the Egyptian exile, Egypt being "the nakedness of the land" [Genesis 42:9] as is known, and as stated: "After the doings of the land of Egypt... shall you not do" [Leviticus 18:3], they being licentiously steeped in sexual depravity, while Israel inversely were meticulously fenced against sexual immorality, as the Sages taught [there was only a single breach (Shelomit bat Dibri) and Scripture publicized it, and she stemmed from the tribe of Dan.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And as stated in Pesikta Rabbati (Piska 15, Parashat HaChodesh): It is written (Psalms 40:6): “Many things have You done, O Lord my God, Your wonderful works and Your thoughts” — all the wonders and thoughts that You devised were so that man would bond with his wife; that is what is written (Genesis 4:25): “And Adam knew his wife again.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Batra 158b: ‘MISHNA: If the house collapsed on a son and upon his mother, and it is unknown who died first, the following claims arise: The mother’s paternal family claims that the son died first, and therefore they inherit from the mother, and the son’s heirs claim that the mother died first and her son inherited from her, and therefore they inherit from the son. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And concerning this occur the exiles and the loss of the Land: namely, because they have not yet attained the spiritual level of "the earth hath He given to the children of men", whose esoteric allusion to the Oral Torah is well known [which is the wisdom of the dwellers of the Land, as our Sages of blessed memory said (Bereshit Rabbah 16): "There is no wisdom like the wisdom of the Land of Israel", and as written (Bava Batra 158b): "The air of the Land of Israel makes one wise", the perfection of the Oral Torah stemming from its side; while Babylonia represents the "rear" (achorayim) of the Oral Torah, this being the Babylonian Talmud which operates in…
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 40:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And it came to pass, that, when the sun went down, and it was dark, behold a smoking furnace, and a burning lamp that passed between those pieces” (Genesis 15:17). “Passing” (over) is not stated, but rather “passed” (avar)— which means Hashem showed him the joy and serenity that Israel will possess then, after all the suffering they endure in the world and are refined in wholeness; therefore the past tense “passed” is used, in that Hashem showed him what had already passed and what will be in the end, giving them a future and hope.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sotah 3a: ‘The Gemara comments: And it stands to reason like the one who says that Rabbi Yishmael was speaking of a spirit of purity, as it is taught in a baraita: “And he warned his wife,” i.e., the issuing of the warning, is optional, that the husband is neither enjoined to nor prohibited from issuing a warning; this is the statement of Rabbi Yishmael. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Which is called 'without his knowledge,' as written: 'Also, that the soul be without knowledge is not good' (Proverbs 19:2), and we find in Shabbat 149b: 'not good' means evil, and this is termed evil. And they said in Sotah 3a: A person does not commit a transgression unless a spirit of folly enters him, which is the 'other god' of whom the Zohar states (Part II, 103a): it is castrated and produces no fruit, and the holy Ari explained that it lacks Da'at (conscious divine awareness), as is known.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And as stated there regarding levirate marriage: “initially her husband and then her son,” so “initially Mother—mother of all—and then Wife.” And this is what the Ari explains in Likutei Torah: that Chavah is numerically the filling of the Name Havayah; and the filling emerges when the primal root point is concealed—the filling initially enfolded within the root point, stepping forth into actuality afterward.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ketubot 110b: ‘The Gemara asks: With regard to this last statement, that this is not the case with regard to a marriage contract: To which part of the baraita is this referring? Rav Mesharshiyya said: It is referring back to the first clause, that if the promissory note mentions Babylonia one pays with Babylonian currency. As taught in the Holy Zohar (Bereishit 16a): Darkness is fire, etc., and this is the mystery of (Genesis 27:1) “and his eyes were dim from seeing”; and in Zohar (Toldot 142a): “‘And the darkness He called Night’—this is Isaac, who drew the night into himself, etc., seeking to envelop himself in awe and cleave to his designated rung, whereupon the night bound itself to him, fulfilling ‘and the darkness He called Night.’”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Deuteronomy 29:22: ‘all its soil devastated by sulfur and salt, beyond sowing and producing, no grass growing in it, just like the upheaval of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which GOD overthrew in fierce anger—’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:44, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Deuteronomy 29:22) to illuminate his teaching here (“whose “whole land is brimstone, and salt, and burning”, “and she became a pillar of salt.” And concerning “Sodomite salt”, our Sages of blessed memory noted Chullin 105b that it blinds the eyes, which mirrors the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For from anger one comes to “coarseness [gassus],” as I wrote above, that the two are one — and they are “branches of the drive for idolatry”; and therefore Yerovam placed the one [calf] in Dan, and there is the “root” of the existence of idolatry in Israel, as they said [in the Sifri] on the verse “lest there be among you a family or a tribe [whose heart turns away]” (Devarim 29:17) — this is the tribe of Dan” — “lest there be among you… a family or a tribe whose heart turns away this day from Hashem” — and the Sifrei comments, “this is the tribe of Dan.”
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “I will make you a terror, and you shall be no more”—in this world; “though you be sought for”—in the World of Souls; “yet shall you never be found”—in the World to Come. Israel, however, existed and are destined eternally to exist; and from where is this known? “Remember Your congregation, which You acquired of old (kedem)”—kedem meaning before the world was created; and they exist now, as it is said: “You stand this day all of you”; and they are destined to endure in the World to Come: “And they shall be Mine, says the Lord of hosts, in that day when I make up My jewels.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Chullin 105b: ‘§ The baraita further teaches that final waters are an obligation. Rav Yehuda, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya, says: For what reason did the Sages say that final waters are an obligation? It is because Sodomite salt is sometimes present, a small amount of which blinds the eyes. Since Sodomite salt could remain on one’s hands, one must wash them after eating. Abaye said: And this type of dangerous salt is present in the proportion of a pinch [korta] in an entire kor of regular salt. Rav Aḥa, son of Rava, said to Rav Ashi: If one measured salt between meals, what is the halakha? Must he wash his hands afterward? He said to him: It is not necessary to say this; he is certainly obligated to do so.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:44, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Chullin 105b) to illuminate his teaching here (“And concerning “Sodomite salt”, our Sages of blessed memory noted Chullin 105b that it blinds the eyes, which mirrors the striking with blindness mentioned above in section 42; for salt represents purifying...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And intellect is drawn after desire, as it is written (Exodus 23:8): 'For bribery blinds, etc.,' because the will bends the intellect. Regarding this they said (Yoma 72b): ''Why is there a purchase price... when there is no heart?' Nevertheless, they also said (Bemidbar Rabbah 10:2): 'The eye sees and the heart covets,' showing that intellect generates desire.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 52:6
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Akin to what we find in the Talmud (Chullin 133a) regarding Abaye, who initially seized priestly gifts from the owners: saying: “I reasoned that I was demonstrating love for the mitzvah; once I heard this verse: 'and he shall give'—teaching that a priest may not seize on his own, I no longer seized, but verbally asked: Give to me; and once I heard that which is taught in the Baraita: The modest withdraw their hands while the gluttons divide, I refrained even from asking or taking altogether.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Leviticus 11:44: ‘For I the ETERNAL am your God: you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I am holy. You shall not make yourselves impure through any swarming thing that moves upon the earth.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:44, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Leviticus 11:44) to illuminate his teaching here (“which is derived from “and you shall be holy” Leviticus 11:44 as written in the chapter Kol HaBasar Chullin 105a and as I wrote elsewhere, which refers to divine assistance from Hashem, blessed be He,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And 'the man of wings' means a master of mitzvot, for there exist two categories of holiness mirroring 'and you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy' (Leviticus 11:44): for 'and you shall be' is the innate sanctity of the Torah scholar, which belongs to his essence, through the Torah his entire body becoming fire, and requires no active striving for holiness; whereas 'and you shall sanctify yourselves' through exertion applies to practitioners of mitzvot, who sanctify themselves from below to achieve a clean body.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And the meaning is as taught in the Zohar (Vayikra 11b): Ten utterances for the work of creation, and Ten Utterances for the Giving of the Torah; meaning that the world did not endure until Hashem spoke explicitly, for as long as it remained in pure thought, no creature held conscious grasp of it. And “speech” is termed when there is perception for each individual, which is called the “toil of hands,” and it was pleasing before them to surrender themselves to be replanted back in their Root.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Chullin 105a: ‘§ Having mentioned the manner of washing hands during a meal, the Gemara discusses another matter concerning washing hands. Rav Idi bar Avin says that Rav Yitzḥak bar Ashyan says: The first waters, i.e., washing of the hands before eating bread, are a mitzva by rabbinic law, but the final waters, washing of the hands upon conclusion of the meal and before reciting Grace after Meals, are an obligation, a more stringent requirement.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:44, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Chullin 105a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in the chapter Kol HaBasar Chullin 105a and as I wrote elsewhere, which refers to divine assistance from Hashem, blessed be He, following the initial washing mayim rishonim,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And so in Moed Katan (9a) on "and joyful and glad of heart" (I Melachim 8:66): "each man's wife conceived a male child"; for although a "merry heart" denotes passion filling the heart, concerning which it is warned: "and that you seek not after your own heart" (Bamidbar 15:39); the ultimate desire of Israel is the Holy One, Who is the "heart of Israel" (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2); and even when engaging in physical union, their intent is purely for Heaven in holiness; having no heart of stone, but a "heart of flesh" to bring forth holy progeny (Pesikta on Yechezkel 11:19).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: It is stated (in Tractate Chullin 60a): At the hour when the Holy One, blessed be He, said [to the trees], “after its kind,” the grasses formulated an a fortiori argument (kal va-chomer) concerning themselves: “If trees, whose natural manner is not to emerge in tangled mixture, were commanded by the Holy One, blessed be He, ‘after its kind,’ we who grow intermingled, all the more so!”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Eruvin 17b: ‘MISHNA: One may arrange upright boards [passin] around a well in the public domain in order to permit drawing water from the well on Shabbat. A well is usually at least four handbreadths wide and ten handbreadths deep. Therefore, it is considered a private domain, and it is prohibited to draw water from it on Shabbat, as that would constitute a violation of the prohibition to carry from a private domain into a public one. The Sages therefore instituted that a virtual partition may be built in the area surrounding the well, so that the enclosed area could be considered a private domain, thus permitting use of the well and carrying of the water within the partitioned area.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:44, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 17b) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written Eruvin 17b. And therefore a quarter-kav of Sodomite salt was placed into the incense Keritot 6a, for the incense is the rectification of the plague that struck over the matter of Peor, which was...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: As they stated [in Eruvin 17b], and see Tosafos there (s.v. lav), and Tosafos [Sanhedrin 63a, s.v. mishum, and 85a, s.v. hikahu]; and regarding a negative command given as a warning for a court execution, it was explained from the Asarah Ma'amaros that it is excluded from this leniency; it seems to me that he said this only when that specific transgression itself was given as a warning for a death penalty, where they warned him for lashes instead of death, for in such a case lies the primary principle of a prohibition given for the warning of a court death penalty [Makkos 13b] and in the Rambam [Hilchos Sanhedrin 18:2], see there.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Meaning that in his power he can gather all creations under his domain, integrating them into himself to stand them upright before the Blessed Name. For in truth holiness resides within all creations, as taught in Eruvin (100b) on Job 35:11: “Rabbi Yochanan said: Had the Torah not been given, we could have learned honesty regarding robbery from the ant, etc.”; yet they lack the power of speech with which to unite with one another, this supreme distinction belonging solely to man, to whom the faculty of speech was given.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Keritot 6a: ‘The Gemara adds: And even according to the one who says that two verses that come as one do teach their common aspect to apply to other cases, here they certainly do not teach that misuse of consecrated property applies to items whose mitzva has been performed. This is due to the fact that there are two terms indicating exclusions with regard to these halakhot, limiting this halakha to those cases. With regard to the removal of the ashes it is written: “And he shall put it.” The word “it” teaches that in this particular case, yes, there is misuse of consecrated property, but with regard to any other matter this prohibition does not apply. With regard to the heifer whose neck is broken it…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:44, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Keritot 6a) to illuminate his teaching here (“And therefore a quarter-kav of Sodomite salt was placed into the incense Keritot 6a, for the incense is the rectification of the plague that struck over the matter of Peor, which was licentiousness; and “the thick...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: "And joy"—this is circumcision (Megillah ibid.), the sanctity of Yesod in guarding the covenant; as I heard regarding the eleven spices of the incense, which correspond to the ten Sefirot, the four explicit biblical spices—stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense Exodus 30:34—representing the central column: Keter, Tiferet, Yesod, and Malchut; and galbanum represents Yesod, whose sweetening is effected through cinnamon, corresponding to Chochmah; and this explains the nine measures of cinnamon (Keritot 6a), Yesod being ninth from below and Chochmah ninth from above.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And the Gemara distinguishes (48a): where words were accompanied by money, the curse of “He who took retribution” applies; where words were unaccompanied by money, it does not apply. The reason being: the ultimate purpose of the Flood was to fortify the legal acquisition of existence; for previously creation held no legal claim, having been brought forth by mere speech (“By the word of the Lord the heavens were made”), and mere verbal agreement does not effect formal acquisition.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ezekiel 8:11: ‘Before them stood seventy of the elders of the House of Israel, with Jaazaniah son of Shaphan standing in their midst. Everyone had a censer in his hand, and a thick cloud of incense smoke ascended.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:44, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Ezekiel 8:11) to illuminate his teaching here (“and “the thick cloud of incense” darkens evil eyes; and likewise it is stated of Sodom: “the smoke kitor of the land like the smoke of a furnace.” And a “quarter-kav” equals six egg-bulks— meaning: the six spatial...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Sichat Malakhei HaSharet, A Note on Angels' Names:7 (§2)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this takes place during the offering of the incense (ketoret), which signifies the binding of all realms together (keshiru d'chula); meaning that all elements are integrated, even Jewish transgressors, as taught in Keritot (6a) that for this reason foul-smelling galbanum was included [wherefore the incense comprises eleven spices, for in the internal alignment Da'at substitutes for Keter, the primary inward service binding within Da'at; yet the elevation of transgressors who are attached externally is rooted solely from the side of Keter, their hidden origin being good, they too joining to crown Hashem, wherefore eleven spices are counted; and this is not its place].
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And I will remember My covenant, which is between Me and you.” This means: from the very circumstance of concealment itself—which resembles a thick cloud, wherein the Blessed Name has hidden Himself from human beings and appears distant from them — from that very condition springs the essential breakthrough of the light of “and I will remember My covenant.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 19:28: ‘and, looking down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and all the land of the Plain, he saw the smoke of the land rising like the smoke of a kiln.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:44, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 19:28) to illuminate his teaching here (“and likewise it is stated of Sodom: “the smoke kitor of the land like the smoke of a furnace.” And a “quarter-kav” equals six egg-bulks— meaning: the six spatial dimensions of lust; for the volume of an egg...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is concealed and lacks a physical base, requiring that it expand upward into the primordial depth of Thought. And in this manner will likewise be understood what I received regarding the secret of "cinnamon nine measures" (Kerisos 6a): alluding to Yesod which is the ninth Sefirah from Above to below, while Chochmah is ninth from below to Above; and the consummate perfection of Yesod is realized when it is drawn, bound, and unified with Chochmah; which aligns precisely with our principle: when one reaches the end, he must return to the beginning.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And upon this premise they likewise built the Tower in the land of Shinar, as explained above (section 34). As stated in the Holy Zohar (Noach 74a): Come and see: concerning Nimrod what is written? ‘And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel’—for from there he took hold to bind himself to an alien domain; and likewise: ‘And they found a plain in the land of Shinar.’”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yoma 80a: ‘All the measures in the Torah connected to eating are the volume of an olive-bulk, except for the amount of food that renders objects impure, because the verse changed its expression in this case, and the Sages altered the measure accordingly. The proof of this, that the Sages gave it a different measure because the verse used different language for it, is from Yom Kippur. Also in the case of Yom Kippur the Sages assigned a different measure because the verse used a different phrase. The Gemara asks: How did the Sages learn that the verse changed its expression? They learned from: “Any soul which shall not be afflicted” (Leviticus 23:29). The verse does not state: Any soul that shall…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:44, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 80a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as our Sages of blessed memory noted Yoma 80a: “the esophagus holds the volume of an egg”; and sexual immorality is likewise described with the terminology of eating: “she eats, and wipes her mouth.””), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Novellae, Rambam, Mamrim 1:3 (§3)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Furthermore: from Eruvin [4a], where Rav said that halakhic measures, partitions, and interpositions are a Halakhah to Moses from Sinai, whereas in Yoma [80a] Rabbi Elazar holds they are rabbinic; see there. Furthermore: from the willow in the Temple, which Rabbi Yochanan in Sukkah [44a] states is a Halakhah to Moses from Sinai, while Abba Shaul disputes him, deriving it from Scripture ("willows of the brook").
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: The Generation of the Flood said unto God (Job 21:14): “Depart from us,” and they did not learn from the Generation of Enosh until He blotted out their memory; even the Generation of the Dispersion did not learn from the early generations, this being what is written: “And the whole earth was of one language and of one speech.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 30:20: ‘Such is the way of an adulteress:She eats, wipes her mouth,And says, “I have done no wrong.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:44, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 30:20) to illuminate his teaching here (““she eats, and wipes her mouth.””), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is the "counterbalance repentance" (teshuvat hamishkal) instituted by the early masters, as is known, for regarding the outward garments of thought, speech, and action, remorse alone suffices, stripping off filthy garments and donning festive robes of Torah and mitzvot. And if the sin was done coldly without any felt pleasure, merely from casting off the yoke and lacking vigilance, then in truth a mere rinsing with cold water suffices, namely channeling his soul's vitality into the yoke of Torah and mitzvot from now on.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And behold, when a person accepts the yoke of Heaven in the Shema, nullifying all personal desires until he has no desire other than His will, seeing Hashem as Singular and Unique, he surrenders himself to consuming fire, for fire cannot tolerate possessions and consumes all, as written (Proverbs 30:16): “and fire says not: Enough”—and in that state of self-negation he is in the aspect of “and one came not near the other.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 19:32: ‘Come, let us make our father drink wine, and let us lie with him, that we may maintain life through our father.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 19:32) to illuminate his teaching here (“Genesis 19:32 “Come, let us make our father drink wine”, for they intended for the sake of a mitzvah, while he intended for sin, as written in Nazir 23a; and therefore the matter was brought about through his...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And it was explained above regarding "like coriander seed (zera gad)": this is the mystery of outside the Land of Israel, where the portion of the lawgiver (Moses) is concealed. The moment Eldad and Medad prophesied his demise at Kivrot HaTa'avah, his burial outside the Land was likewise portended: through the craving for food came his physical death, and through the sin of the tongue came his burial outside.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As taught in the Gemara (Berakhot 57a): “Wine—one drinks it and it is beneficial, another drinks it and it is harmful; a Torah scholar always benefits.” Meaning, even prior to divine illumination when a person still dwells in darkness, if his heart yearns passionately for redemption, holy counsel emerges within him allowing worldly goods to elevate his service.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Nazir 23a: ‘The Gemara raises a difficulty: Is it comparable? We said one path; i.e., two people follow the same path by performing the very same action with two different outcomes; whereas here there are two paths. Each person engaged in sexual intercourse with a different relative and therefore they cannot be said to have followed the same path. Rather, it is comparable to Lot and his two daughters, who were with him. They, who intended to engage in sexual intercourse with him for the sake of a mitzva, as they thought that the entire world was destroyed and wished to preserve the human race, are described in the first part of the verse: “And the just walk in them.” He who intended to act for the…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Nazir 23a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in Nazir 23a; and therefore the matter was brought about through his drunkenness. And our Sages of blessed memory noted in Eruvin 65a: once a person reaches the drunkenness of Lot—his legal status is like...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the entire descent of the soul of Mashiach into the world transpired through such paradoxes: that there should be an external thought of bodily lust, yet inwardly directed for the sake of Heaven; and this Mashiach will clarify regarding all the lusts of Israel: that everything was sovereignly ordered from the six days of Creation by the Blessed Name!
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 57:6–7
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Until he departed from the boundaries entirely in his arrogant confidence; this is an absolute voiding of the transaction, greater than a sixth. “The seller was defrauded in less than a sixth” is as in (Psalms 78:36): “Nevertheless they flattered Him with their mouth, and lied unto Him with their tongue”, which is merely from the lip outward; and nonetheless: “But He, being full of compassion, forgives iniquity, and destroys not” (ibid. 38), as brought in the Talmud (Ta'anit 8a).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Eruvin 65a: ‘The Gemara raises an objection to this argument from the following baraita: With regard to one who is intoxicated, his acquisition is a binding acquisition; that is, he cannot retract the transaction when he is sober, and similarly, his sale is a binding sale. Moreover, if he committed a transgression for which he is liable to receive the death penalty, he is executed; and if the offense is punishable by lashes, he is flogged. The principle is that he is like a sober person in all matters, except that he is exempt from prayer. Therefore, even if the people of Israel are considered drunk, they are nonetheless responsible for their actions.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 65a) to illuminate his teaching here (“And our Sages of blessed memory noted in Eruvin 65a: once a person reaches the drunkenness of Lot—his legal status is like an imbecile; and we hold as established halakhah in Chullin 88a and Gittin 22b that regarding...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For "wine gladdens the heart of man" (Tehillim 104:15), and "a man is obligated to become intoxicated on Purim until he does not know" (Megillah 7b); this being profound intoxication wherein one is legally exempt from all commandments (Eruvin 65a); forgetting all worldly burdens through the fog of wine, and not through absolute spiritual reality.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And as stated (Midrash Tehillim 19): In two matters the nations concede: Shabbat and the Resurrection of the Dead. And it is taught in Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit 11:5) that on Shabbat the dead cannot be summoned up by a necromancer (ba'al ov). Therefore the nations concede to this as well; for a necromancer raises a person through that unrectified drive he retained in this world concerning some matter, leaving within that departed soul a craving to return to this world to straighten what was crooked, as taught in the Holy Zohar (Beshalach 54a) regarding the Resurrection of the Dead.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Chullin 88a: ‘§ The mishna teaches that one is obligated to cover blood that spurts outside the pit over which the animal was slaughtered, or onto the wall, and blood that remained on the slaughtering knife. With regard to this halakha, the Sages taught in a baraita: The verse states: “And he shall cover it” (Leviticus 17:13), which teaches that one is obligated to cover blood that spurted and blood that remained on the slaughtering knife. Rabbi Yehuda said: When is this the halakha? When there is no blood except that blood. But if there is other blood that is not that blood, one is exempt from covering it.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Chullin 88a) to illuminate his teaching here (“and we hold as established halakhah in Chullin 88a and Gittin 22b that regarding a deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor, the intention of an adult standing over them is legally effective for them as well; and therefore...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And therefore he prayed "Create for me a pure heart, etc." For one who blemished the Covenant through actual sin in deed cannot rectify the root of lust completely so as to grasp the Tree of Life and rectify the Serpent's instigation, except through the repentance worthy of covering over all his deeds (Zohar III, 214b); meaning like the repentance of Rabbi Elazar ben Dordaya [in Avodah Zarah 17a] whose soul departed amid the bitterness of his heart; and likewise one who attains this through the sheer intensity of love, like Israel at the Giving of the Torah as mentioned above.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: This parallels the halakhic principle regarding forbidden items of benefit (issurei hana'ah), which are disqualified from mitzvot requiring a physical measure because “their measure is considered crushed to powder” (kittutei mikatat shiureih), yet valid for mitzvot requiring no measure; as in Chullin (89a) regarding the ash of a condemned city being valid for covering blood: for a lulav a minimum size is required, which crushing invalidates; while for covering blood, being crushed to fine dust is superior.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Gittin 22b: ‘MISHNA: Anyone is qualified to write a bill of divorce, even a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor. Additionally, a woman may write her own bill of divorce and give it to her husband so that he can present it to her. And a man may write his own receipt, which must be given to him by the woman to confirm that he has paid her the value of her marriage contract. This is because the ratification of a bill of divorce is only through its signatories, and it is irrelevant who wrote it.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Gittin 22b) to illuminate his teaching here (“and we hold as established halakhah in Chullin 88a and Gittin 22b that regarding a deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor, the intention of an adult standing over them is legally effective for them as well; and therefore...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Which is the nature of the feminine/receptive archetype in its state of yearning: "There are three things that are never satisfied..." Proverbs 30:15, finding satisfaction not in final attainment, but in the yearning itself: "and your desire shall be to your husband" Genesis 3:16, in seeking divine completion. And this is the rung of David who proclaimed: "seek His face continually" Psalms 105:4, and many similar verses, Rather, he will seek only through requesting and inquiring continually, for he has no satiety of finding whatsoever, ever, for “they shall not be satisfied”.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Yet because His benevolent Will yearned to bestow good upon His creatures, He established in this world that every entity be bounded by measure and boundary (and these matters are profound; examine the introduction to the holy book Beit Yaakov [Sha'ar HaEmunah], page 101, and you will understand).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sanhedrin 70a: ‘Rabbi Yitzḥak says: What is the meaning of that which is written: “Look not upon wine when it is red” (Proverbs 23:31)? Look not upon wine that reddens the faces of the wicked in this world when they drink it, and whitens their faces, i.e., embarrasses them, in the World-to-Come. Rava says that this is how the verse should be understood: “Look not upon wine that reddens [yitaddam]” means: Look not upon wine, as it leads to bloodshed [dam], indicating that one who drinks wine will end up committing an act of killing or will be killed because of it.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 70a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as our Sages of blessed memory noted in Sanhedrin 70a; therefore, through the very thing with which they corrupted, were they rectified, so that through it should emerge the soul of the Messiah, who rectifies the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: In that very matter in which a person's deficiency lies, in that exact thing and through it itself is his true spiritual virtue, in the spirit of what our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Sanhedrin 70a) on "and they sewed fig leaves": through the very medium in which they corrupted were they rectified. And along these lines is likewise what our Sages of blessed memory stated (Yerushalmi Berakhot 2:4): On the very day the Temple was destroyed, the Messiah was born.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: So that in reward for this restraint, even when Hashem conducts His world with infinite light in the Sabbath of the World to Come, the people of Israel will maintain distinct existence. And as stated in Sanhedrin (92a): “Those years in which the Holy One will renew His world, what do the righteous do? The Holy One makes wings for them and they soar above the waters, etc.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 57a: ‘The tanna who recited mishnayot before Rabbi Yoḥanan taught: One who sees any kind of drink in a dream it is a good omen, except for wine, as there is one who drinks it in a dream and it is a good omen for him, and there is one who drinks it in a dream and it is a bad omen for him. The Gemara elaborates: There is one who drinks wine and it is a good omen for him, as it is stated: “And wine that makes glad the heart of man” (Psalms 104:15), and there is one who drinks it in a dream and it is a bad omen for him, as it is stated: “Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish and wine unto the bitter in soul” (Proverbs 31:6).’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 57a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in HaRoeh Berakhot 57a: there is one who drinks it and thrives, etc.; for it contains good, as written in Eruvin 65a: “Until I drink... my mind is not clear”,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For excess regurgitates even what was previously internalized, matching: "Give me neither poverty nor riches" (Proverbs 30:8)—meaning excessive intellectual wealth that detaches from reality uproots everything. So too with wine in Berakhot (57a): "There is one who drinks it and it is good for him, and one who drinks it and it is bad for him," for Torah is likened to wine (life for those on the right, poison for those on the left).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 42:6
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this explains why in the eighteen blessings of Shemoneh Esreh no explicit blessing for children is formulated, except in the blessing 'Upon the Righteous', where prayer for children is alluded to: “and grant a good reward”—alluding to children, as written (Psalms 127:3): “Lo, children are a heritage of Hashem; the fruit of the womb is a reward”; and the conclusion of the blessing is: “Blessed are You Hashem, the stay and trust of the righteous”, and children are titled a 'staff' (mishan).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Eruvin 65a: ‘Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi said that Rav said: Anyone whose mind is unsettled should not pray, as it is stated: When distressed, one should not issue decisions. The Gemara relates that Rabbi Ḥanina, on a day that he was angry, would not pray, as he said that it is written: When distressed, one should not issue decisions. The Gemara similarly relates that Mar Ukva, on a day of a south wind, would not venture out to the court, for this hot and harsh wind would disturb his usual clarity of mind.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 65a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in Eruvin 65a: “Until I drink... my mind is not clear”, alluding to the Tree of Knowledge in the holy good that lies within it; and so the Torah is compared to wine,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: [And so is the order of study: by day one studies the Written Torah which bestows, and by night the Oral Torah which receives (see Shemot Rabbah, Ki Tisa), as is known that the Oral Torah is built upon the Written Torah and receives from it. And in Eruvin (65a): "Your halachot are sharp—for they were developed by day," shining like the sun, for halachah requires lucid clarity like a clear day with a northern wind; which is the capacity of reception, serving as a fitting vessel for the words of Torah.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As elucidated in Mei HaShiloach (Vol. 1, Mishpatim) on Shabbat (69b): One walking in the wilderness who lost count of Shabbat: Chiyya bar Rav says, he observes one day and counts six; Rav Huna says, he counts six and observes one day. A youth whose heart is unrefined (Chiyya bar Rav) should not pray for worldly pleasures, but surrender all desire beforehand so Hashem is the beginner and completer, observing Shabbat first and then counting six; while Rav Huna—possessing rich spiritual wealth, his heart purified from alien cravings —.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 88b: ‘With regard to the revelation at Sinai, Rabbi Yoḥanan said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “The Lord gives the word; the women that proclaim the tidings are a great host” (Psalms 68:12)? And, similarly, the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught with regard to the verse: “Behold, is My word not like fire, declares the Lord, and like a hammer that shatters a rock?” (Jeremiah 23:29). Just as this hammer breaks a stone into several fragments, so too, each and every utterance that emerged from the mouth of the Holy One, Blessed be He, divided into seventy…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 88b) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in Shabbat 88b and Yoma 72b; and “Death and life are in the power of the tongue”, which corresponds to the Torah; and “A soothing tongue is a tree of life”,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Is literally absolute Unity exactly as before the world was created, which constitutes total attachment unto the very expiration of the soul, in the sense of "my soul failed when he spoke," since he perceives that he is not an entity detached from His Essence; and therefore with every single utterance at Sinai their soul departed, and the Holy One, blessed be He, brought down the dew of resurrection [Shabbat 88b] to return them to the stature of a created being, and this explains: "Did ever a people hear...
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 9:8
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And what is the power of fire? That it shatters and pulverizes every entity into fragments, not annihilating the substance completely but crumbling it into particles, as indicated in the Talmud (Sukkah 31b): that a lulav of an asherah is invalid, and in Chullin (89a): ash of an asherah is valid for covering the blood, proving that we do not say it is considered non-existent, for if it were non-existent, with what is he covering the blood as the Torah commanded?!

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yoma 72b: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “And this is the Torah which Moses put [sam] before the children of Israel” (Deuteronomy 4:44)? The word sam is written with the letter sin and means put; it is phonetically similar to the word sam written with the letter samekh, meaning a drug. This use of this word therefore alludes to the following: If one is deserving, the Torah becomes a potion [sam] of life for him. If one is not deserving, the Torah becomes a potion of death for him. And this idea is what Rava said: For one who is skillful in his study of Torah and immerses himself in it with love, it is a potion of life; but for one who is not skillful in…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 72b) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in Shabbat 88b and Yoma 72b; and “Death and life are in the power of the tongue”, which corresponds to the Torah; and “A soothing tongue is a tree of life”,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Words of Torah, moreover, intrinsically gladden the heart, as it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:19): "Wisdom strengthens the wise," imbuing him with strength and fortitude, and therefore they taught (Yoma 72b): "If he did not merit, it becomes a potion of death, etc.," because wisdom can engender levity and arrogance within him, and he is termed 'wise to do evil,' Heaven forbid.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And the inner meaning is: Rabbi Eliezer measures from the primal inception of being, for instantly by the word of Hashem all was constituted, yet creation's face was still turned upward toward its Emanator—and this Rabbi Eliezer designates as creation; whereas Rabbi Yehoshua measures from the moment creation turned its countenance downward to bestow life outward into the world.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 18:21: ‘Death and life are in the power of the tongue;Those who love it will eat its fruit.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 18:21) to illuminate his teaching here (“and “Death and life are in the power of the tongue”, which corresponds to the Torah; and “A soothing tongue is a tree of life”, which is the Torah as written in Eruvin 54a;”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua:28 (§5)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For his root is not truly so; only through effort alone did he merit this, which is the fruit of the Torah: dominion without the eternal crown. But Othniel merited the essence of Torah—dialectical study—Moses' root given generously, transmitting his intrinsic power of Torah rather than its derivative fruit; wherefore Othniel restored those three roots forgotten in hundreds and thousands, rectifying both the internal faculties producing doubts and the encompassing lights.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 11:5–6
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Behold it is in Hashem's great power to bequeath eternal life without any limit! And even when Hashem's salvation in eternal life reached him, he served Hashem even within that, because he believed in Hashem, blessed be He, that there exists eternal life with Hashem to bequeath to those who love Him which is beyond human ability to grasp intellectually; and whatever salvation he received in Hashem was considered by him as mere temporal achievement compared to the infinite salvation still remaining within Hashem's power.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 15:4: ‘A healing tongue is a tree of life,But a devious one makes for a broken spirit.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 15:4) to illuminate his teaching here (“and “A soothing tongue is a tree of life”, which is the Torah as written in Eruvin 54a; as noted above that through that which they corrupted are they rectified, and as our Sages of blessed memory stated Bereishit...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the Sabbath corresponds to Malchut, the mouth and the faculty of speech; wherefore all agree the Torah was given on the Sabbath (Shabbat 86b), Torah being the Tree of Life healing the tongue; for one who immerses in Torah has all his conversation elevated into Torah. And this is the healing of the loquacious tongue through Torah, turning his body into fire, as in Chagigah (27a): "Is not My word like fire, says Hashem" Jeremiah 23:29; through vital Torah speech the permutation of his soul-root becoming pure burning fire.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For “and it was so” indicates that it received the full completion of active power, while its omission shows that active capacity was not yet fully finalized. Likewise, at the initial creation of animal life and man “and it was so” is absent, writing instead: “And God created the great sea monsters,” and “And God created man”; for “and it was so” indicates an organic protrusion from within existing elements, like fruit emerging from a tree; whereas light, living animal soul, and man who is a speaking spirit—all three are absolute novelties, and therefore “and it was so” is omitted.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Eruvin 54a: ‘Having expounded the verse “For they are life to those who find them” as referring to the Torah, the Gemara cites another teaching related to this verse that praises the Torah. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: One who is walking along the way without a companion and is afraid should engage in Torah study, as it is stated with regard to the words of Torah: “For they shall be a graceful wreath [livyat ḥen] for your head, and chains about your neck” (Proverbs 1:9). The word livyat is understood here as a reference to levaya, accompaniment, so that the verse is interpreted to mean that Torah is a graceful accompaniment to one who is traveling.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 54a) to illuminate his teaching here (“which is the Torah as written in Eruvin 54a; as noted above that through that which they corrupted are they rectified, and as our Sages of blessed memory stated Bereishit Rabbah 9:7: “Very good”—this is the evil...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Man in this world needs companionship, just as they stated in Berakhot (6b): "The entire world was created solely to accompany this one," inferring from this that he requires the company of created beings. And our Sages of blessed memory taught (Eruvin 54a): "One who travels on the road without an escort should engage in Torah," and this entire world is termed 'walking on the road,' as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Sotah 21a) on the verse 'When you walk, it will lead you, etc.' – in this world.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As taught in the Holy Zohar (Vayeira 109a) on the verse (Job 37:12): “And it is turned round about by His guidance, that they may do whatever He commands them” — according to the actions of human beings, as they act, etc.; Rabbi Eliezer said: “And it is turned round about”—the Holy One, blessed be He, orchestrates turning circumstances, bringing situations into the world to be established; and after people assume those structures are fixed, the Holy One overturns those very affairs from how they were initially.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 9:7: ‘Rabbi Naḥman bar Shmuel bar Naḥman said in the name of Rav Shmuel bar Naḥman: “Behold it was very good” – this is the good inclination; “and behold it was very good” – this is the evil inclination. Is the evil inclination, then, very good? This is a rhetorical question. Rather, were it not for the evil inclination, a man would never build a house, would never marry a wife, would never beget children, and would never engage in commerce. Likewise, Solomon says: “[And I have considered all toil and all excelling in work,] that it is each man’s envy of his counterpart” (Ecclesiastes 4:4).’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 9:7) to illuminate his teaching here (“and as our Sages of blessed memory stated Bereishit Rabbah 9:7: “Very good”—this is the evil inclination, in which resides the core of rectification. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Bereishit Rabbah, Parashah 9): "'Very good'—this is the evil inclination," because from it the dawn of light is drawn, for it will be revealed that 'darkness shall cover, etc.' applies only to the idolaters, whereas within Israel the evil inclination holds no true dominion at all, since at the inner point truly designated by the name of Israel, sin never reaches; which is exemplified by 'a myrtle standing among thorny hedges' (Sanhedrin 44a).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Subsequently that vivid light is concealed, and man must begin clarifying himself through rigorous self-restraint, toiling in Torah and prayer, until he pierces the concealment, draws close to the Blessed Name, and becomes bound to Him eternally. And this explains Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit 3:4): Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said: This teaches that the Holy One cloaked Himself in it as with a garment, and the splendor of His majesty radiated from one end of the world to the other, etc..

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yevamot 65b: ‘GEMARA: From where are these matters derived, that a woman is not obligated in the mitzva to be fruitful and multiply?
