Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And according to this, no difficulty arises from the verse "And God blessed them," wherein He addressed both of them with "be fruitful and multiply" (Yevamot 65b): for it was only when woman was stricken with the curse "and he shall rule over you" that she entered the status of deficiency, as explained above [and this occurred because she caused the introduction of mortality into the world, which is a deficiency in the very spiritual form of Man; unlike eating and reproduction which are merely physical characteristics of matter; therefore she was penalized measure for measure to become the embodiment of deficiency].
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them: Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth.” Although to Adam it was already commanded “Be fruitful and multiply,” here it is an enduring blessing. As in Likutei Torah of the Ari on Genesis 2:5: — “Siacḥ” is an acronym for Shem, Yephet, Cham; “for the Lord had not caused it to rain”—the Flood had not yet occurred.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 3:16: ‘And to the woman [God] said,“I will greatly expandYour toil—and your pregnancies;In hardship shall you bear children.Yet your urge shall be for your husband,And his will shall prevail over yours.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 3:16) to illuminate his teaching here (“and as written: “and your desire shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you.” Therefore the entire building of the House of David— unfolded through the proactive initiative of women, such as the daughters...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Which is in the manner taught in Eruvin (54b): regarding Torah scholars: "all their conversation is Torah", for each according to his root, such is his speech. Nonetheless, our Sages of blessed memory noted (Ketubot 64b): "a man's lust is greater, and go and learn from the market of harlots, etc."; because God already killed the female Leviathan after the sin, in that she was cursed: "and your desire shall be to your husband", such that she does not demand intimacy with her mouth.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For has He not warned: “You shall not take vengeance nor bear any grudge,” and Hashem observes the Torah first; how then does the Torah obligate punishment upon a past sin, when it says: “You shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge”? Rather, Hashem certainly does not punish for the past, but for the present—for one's deeds at that moment: for once a person has become corrupted and rooted in sin, he is prone to sin continuously, and is punished for the present desire to sin harbored within his heart.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ecclesiastes 10:11: ‘If the snake bites because no spell was uttered, no advantage is gained by the trained charmer.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Ecclesiastes 10:11) to illuminate his teaching here (“on the verse “If the serpent bites, etc.”, and he was the inciter toward the Tree of Knowledge; and David stands countering slander as I wrote elsewhere and as written above in section 27, and this is not the place...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: After the manner of "the mouse lying upon gold dinars" (Sanhedrin 29b); this being the root of the Serpent who bites without deriving any pleasure (Koheles Rabbah 10:11 on Koheles 10:11). And therefore through monetary greed comes the ultimate forgetting of Hashem more than through any other appetite; as stated in Parashat Eikev: "lest when you have eaten and are full... and your silver and your gold is multiplied... then your heart be lifted up, and you forget Hashem your God" (Devarim 8:12–14).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And from Hashem’s vantage point, it is as taught in the Talmud (Chagigah 12a): “At the time the Holy One, blessed be He, created His world, it expanded continuously like two balls of warp-threads,” meaning that from Hashem’s side existence expands boundlessly without limit or end; and when Hashem uttered “Let there be,” it kept expanding, and only for the sake of the vessel of creation did Hashem say “Dai” (Enough!), thereby imposing these finite borders.

A connection is thus made between the act of speech and the act of circumcision, being two forms of creation and transformation according to the SY’s thought. Another association between language, mouth, and genitals, though the connection (if any) with the SY is unclear, is found in…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this kabbalistic teaching (Sefer Yetzirah 1:3) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in Sefer Yetzirah 1:3, therefore their pursuit was to achieve rectification through this very physical desire when purified and directed toward a holy mitzvah; and mediated through women,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the “five kav” — or “three” — of R’ Yochanan is [the span] from Gevurah to Yesod, or corresponding to Netzach-Hod-Yesod; and this is less than R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei, whose clarification of holiness reached to the root; and Rav Pappa’s [was] less still, for the generations “go and diminish.” And each one who was himself engaged in this matter [of guarding the bris] could discern and apprehend the rung of the one before him — who was also of the character of his rung, and somewhat greater than him.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And call the Sabbath a delight (oneg)”—delight means that man yearns exclusively for the illumination of the Countenance of the Blessed Name; and the exact reverse of oneg is nega , as stated in Sefer Yetzirah (2:4): “There is nothing in goodness higher than oneg, and nothing in evil lower than nega,” and nega signifies that a person fled from before his Master, as stated in the Holy Zohar (Tazria 49b): “the shutting off of supernal light.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 48b: ‘The baraita with regard to Grace after Meals continues: I only have a Torah source for Grace after Meals. From where is the obligation to recite the blessing of the Torah derived? Several answers are offered: Rabbi Yishmael said: It is derived through an a fortiori inference from Grace after Meals: Over food, which is an aspect of temporal life, one recites a blessing, all the more so one recites a blessing over the Torah, which is eternal life. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Naḥmani, the student of Rabbi Yishmael, says in the name of Rabbi Yishmael: This a fortiori inference is not necessary, as this halakha can be derived from the same verse from which Grace after Meals is derived, as it states: “For…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 48b) to illuminate his teaching here (“who are talkative and conversational, as our Sages noted Berakhot 48b; and through wine, as written in Vayikra Rabbah 12:1: “Who has babbling? Who has wounds without cause? Those who tarry long over wine.””), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is the purpose of reciting a blessing before every action: to dedicate all of one's deeds to God, as it is written: "In all your ways acknowledge Him" (Proverbs 3:6), as Maimonides explained. And this consciousness is achieved through the blessing; as the Sages stated regarding the qualifying age for a minor: a child who knows to Whom we recite blessings (Berakhot 48a).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 11:8 (§3)
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Advancing at every moment to a realm where he had not yet been. And in the final trial this exact principle was tested within eternal life, and he offered his only son as a burnt-offering unto Hashem, for he believed in Hashem that the salvation in his hand was as nothing compared to the eternal life remaining with Hashem which is boundless, to the extent that the eternal life in his hand relative to that with Hashem is like the difference between temporal life and eternal life.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Vayikra Rabbah 12:1: ‘“Wine or intoxicating drink you shall not drink, you and your sons with you, upon your entry into the Tent of Meeting, and you will not die; an eternal statute for your generations” (Leviticus 10:9). “Wine or intoxicating drink you shall not drink.” That is what is written: “Do not look upon wine in its redness [ki yitadam]” (Proverbs 23:31). What is ki yitadam? Because [ki] he will desire [yitaveh] the blood [dam] of a menstruant and the blood of a zava. “As to one who directs his eye to the cup [bakos]” (Proverbs 23:31), bakis is written, it is a euphemism, as it is written: “There will be one purse [kis] for us all” (Proverbs 1:14). “All paths are upright” (Proverbs 23:31);…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Vayikra Rabbah 12:1) to illuminate his teaching here (“and through wine, as written in Vayikra Rabbah 12:1: “Who has babbling? Who has wounds without cause? Those who tarry long over wine.””), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: There is no personal path that does not contain crooked turns, only that in a man's own eyes it appears straight, as written in Proverbs 21:2: "Every way of a man is right in his own eyes"; for through physical desires one inevitably twists his pathways, which form hidden pits making the road uneven, as written in Vayikra Rabbah (12:1) on the verse "it goes down smoothly" (Proverbs 23:31): for to one who walks uprightly, all illicit temptations appear like a level plain (Yoma 75a).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “These are the generations of Noah, etc.” It is written (Psalms 92:1): “A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day.” “Mizmor” (psalm) denotes constriction, related to the expression “you shall not prune (lo tizmor)” (Leviticus 25:4), for through self-constriction man gains an enduring advantage, ensuring he will not be dissolved in the future when the light of the Holy One—which resembles a blazing torch—is unveiled, as taught in Pesachim (8a).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 23:29: ‘Who cries, “Woe!” who, “Alas!”;Who has quarrels, who complaints;Who has wounds without cause;Who has bleary eyes?’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:45, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 23:29) to illuminate his teaching here (““Who has babbling? Who has wounds without cause? Those who tarry long over wine.””), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And from the side of emunah — which is what Israel believe in a general way, without clear apprehension — one believes even in what he does not apprehend at all, for that is the very definition of faith; and this is the sense of “Your faithfulness in the nights” — in the darkness and concealment of the clear light, when one makes use of faith, unlike the morning’s “emes v’yatziv [true and firm],” for “truth” is a thing wholly clarified to him, which cannot be argued against, being revealed to the eye — and it is from the side of the apprehension of chochmah, as they said [Berachos 5b], “there is no truth except Torah.”
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For in the future Hashem will bestow those very blessings without any toil, as in Ketubot (111b) on Psalms 72:16: fruits will drop effortlessly and wine flow without human effort. And this is what the Midrash meant by “He sanctified it with the manna”—hinting that Hashem Himself sanctifies Shabbat directly, rather than through human initiative; “and He blessed it with the manna”—infusing the manna on Shabbat with all exquisite tastes beyond the weekdays; and a third wonder: that while on weekdays it spoiled if left overnight, on Shabbat its freshness endured unspoiled.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 20:2: ‘Abraham said of Sarah his wife, “She is my sister.” So King Abimelech of Gerar had Sarah brought to him.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:46, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 20:2) to illuminate his teaching here (“(Genesis 20:2) “And Abimelech sent, etc.”, for with the impending birth of Isaac, the dread of Hashem began spreading throughout the world, to the point that there was almost no room left to commit evil, and as...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: "At his left"—corrupt Gevurah in anger, envy, and rivalry, designated as a "thousand," the highest named number (Ramban on Genesis 20:16). A bounded count taken to the extreme uses "thousand," while that transcending count takes "ten thousand." Thus officers extend to a thousand, while over ten thousand reigns a king. And since the inclination for desire is "very good" (Midrash HaNe'elam, Zohar I:138a), remaining in the future refined—for without it love of Torah would vanish—being boundless, its spread in evil is likewise manifold.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And when they expand excessively, even their guardian angels suffer, sinking into that attribute without restraint, unable to return to the supreme Will; dragging their angelic prince into dark garments to oppose the divine Will, the angels powerless to arrest them. As said to Abimelech: “Yea, I also withheld you from sinning against Me; therefore I did not allow you to touch her”; the Zohar noting: through the sins of the nation below, their supernal prince is deposed from dominion.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Pirkei Avot 3:1: ‘Akabyah ben Mahalalel said: mark well three things and you will not come into the power of sin: know from where you come, and where you are going, and before whom you are destined to give an account and reckoning. From where do you come? From a putrid drop. Where are you going? To a place of dust, of worm and of maggot. Before whom you are destined to give an account and reckoning? Before the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:46, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Pirkei Avot 3:1) to illuminate his teaching here (“and as written: Akavya said: Contemplate, etc., and you will not come into the grip of sin. And because our Sages of blessed memory stated (Yoma 39b): “He who comes to defile himself—they open the door for him”,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: The Torah being the spice against the inclination (Bava Batra 16a; Kiddushin 30b), and likewise reverent Awe, as taught in the Sifrei: "If you come to rebel, know before Whom you stand in awe," and as taught by Akavya ben Mahalalel (Avot 3:1): "Reflect upon before Whom you are destined to give an accounting, and you will not come into the grip of sin," which is the awe of retribution [and as stated (Berakhot 33b): "Everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven," which is placed in human hands.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 2:4 (§2)
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Because they did not endure, judgment not being sweetened by judgment, etc.' And this befell them because they sought the inner chambers without the outer chambers, wherefore they lacked an ordered path through which to enter, as brought in the Talmud (Shabbat 31b). And from those shattered worlds was built the World of Rectification (Tikkun).
